The real difference is which side they represent and what problem they solve.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px 0;"><span><span>A forward proxy sits next to the client. Your laptop sends a request, the proxy forwards it out, and the destination never sees your real IP. Corporate networks use this to enforce policy, block sites, and cache traffic.</span><br><br><span>A reverse proxy sits next to the server. The client has no idea how many machines are behind it. The proxy decides who handles the request, terminates TLS, and keeps your backend off the public internet. NGINX and HAProxy are commonly used here, typically paired with a load balancer in front.</span><br><br><span>An API gateway is a reverse proxy that does more than route traffic. It also handles auth, rate limits, API keys, versioning, and request shaping. Without it, each microservice has to implement its own version of validation, throttling logic, and request logging.</span><br><br><span>A forward proxy represents the client, a reverse proxy represents the server, and an API gateway is what you add when ten services need the same authentication and rate limiting rules applied consistently.</span><br><br><span>In most real systems, all three are running at different layers. The forward proxy filters outbound traffic, the reverse proxy fronts the application servers, and the API gateway sits in front of your APIs to enforce policies before requests reach them.</span><br><br><span>Over to you: What's your proxy + gateway combo? Always interesting to see what teams pair together.</span></span></p></div></div><div class="postscript-placeholder" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;font-size: Symbol';font-weight: 400;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em><span>The Pulse is a series covering events, insights, and trends within Big Tech and startups.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>Today, we cover:</span></em></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><em><strong><span>Meta can’t stop the “resignation-wave” it triggered. </span></strong><span>In what was predictable: Meta’s layoffs and forced reassignments pushed engineers not impacted by either to look for a new job. Meta is now offering large equity retainers to keep these folks, and it doesn’t seem to be working.</span></em></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><em><strong><span>Grok Bot: the “OpenClaw moment” for managed AI agents? </span></strong><span>The Cursor team built and released a generic AI harness that feels like the “Codex experience, but for knowledge work.” I tried it out, automated a lot of my daily workflows, and am a massive fan. More AI vendors will surely copy this harness.</span></em></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>Apologies for this week’s The Pulse arriving a day later than usual – our family got a puppy this week – who is beyond adorable –, but has kept me up a few nights, indirectly delaying this week’s The Pulse. We’re getting into a rhythm, so things should be back to normal, looking ahead.</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>1. Meta unable to stop the “resignation-wave” it triggered?</span></h2><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Two months ago, I </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2daf997f-f3e0-452d-b560-8cf3886669b1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>covered</span></a><span> how Meta seemingly deliberately started destroying its once-standout engineering organization. The company did 10% layoffs at a time when revenue and profits hit an all-time high, and reassigned about 20-30% of software engineers to data labeling with basically no notice.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The result was that a good chunk of software engineers at Meta – even those not reassigned – were starting to interview elsewhere:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em><span>Why so many engineers at Meta are looking for a way out, visualised. Source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2daf997f-f3e0-452d-b560-8cf3886669b1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>Why is Meta destroying its engineering organization?</span></a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I said – and still maintain – that the layoffs were an unenforced, self-inflicted error on Meta’s part. Coupled with forced reassignment, they struck disaster. And I’ve now gathered new details that confirm that Meta is bleeding top engineering and product management talent:</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Some layoffs reversed, in the 11th hour</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the UK, mass layoffs require a notification to those </span><em><span>potentially</span></em><span> affected, before the cuts can happen. A few weeks after this notification, a good chunk of folks were “un-notified,” I confirmed. But those on notice had already started to look for jobs, obviously.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Retainer equity grants offered to IC6+ engineers resigning</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Meta started to offer large retainer equity grants to those resigning and leaving for Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI: a practice not done before. Talking with long-time Meta engineers, Meta simply didn't make counteroffers or negotiate when an engineer handed in their resignation. But this practice has been abandoned. Here’s a story of a senior, long-tenured engineer I confirmed to have happened:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>This dev was force-reassigned to one of the AI data labeling teams</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>They thought “oh no, this is not what I want to do” and started to interview</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Got a Google offer, but compensation was below their current one. Google basically lowballed them.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Decided to leave anyway. Told their new manager they are resigning.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>New manager asked for some time, then presented a large, one-off, retainer equity grant, vesting over 3 years</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The engineer went back to Google, telling the company unfortunately, they are a key engineer and showed them the retainer amount Meta is paying for them to stay</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Google upped their offer, out-bidding Meta’s retainer offer</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The engineer who was desperate to leave – even for lower compensation! – was thrilled, and happily left for Google.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Retainer equity seems to be offered for most IC6 engineers who resigned in the last few weeks. </span></strong><span>I talked with seven such people, who were all IC6 (staff-level engineer) and IC7 (principal-level engineers), who shared more details. They are not aware of IC4 (mid-level engineer) or IC5 (senior-level engineers) getting such offers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Retainer equity offered is $400K to $1M+</span></strong><span>, and vests over 3 years, for the folks who got these offers. The $1M+ offers were all for engineers with Anthropic or OpenAI offers, and I confirmed a $400K and a $600K grant for engineers with an offer for other, smaller AI startups.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A current Meta engineer who is interviewing asked me if these folks needed to present their offer letter to get a counteroffer. I asked two of these folks with counteroffers, and neither had to do so, but they both indicated they were handing in their resignation. Upon receiving this notification, their director, together with HR, offered a discretionary retainer equity, should they stay.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Anthropic and OpenAI on a hiring spree from Meta</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Anthropic and OpenAI seem to be on a hiring spree, signing Meta engineers that Meta wants to retain now that it is too late! I have confirmed that three engineers who received an offer from Anthropic were also offered large, $1M+ equity grants (vesting over 4 years) as counter-offers to stay. Two out of the three rejected it and joined Anthropic, and the third one initially accepted the offer and then still left for Anthropic a month later, forfeiting this grant.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>OpenAI is having similar success, and the two AI labs seem to be the main destination for now ex-Meta engineers to bounce to. It makes sense: these companies can match Meta’s total compensation, and although neither OpenAI nor Anthropic is publicly traded, both companies organize secondary equity sales, and their respective IPOs are likely to happen in 3-12 months’ time.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>AI startups also successful in hiring infra experts from Meta</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I had an in-depth discussion with another long-tenured AI infra engineer at Meta, who was considering whether to stay, or to go. This person wrote up their situation, and shared it with me, writing:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“With the current situation at Meta (layoffs, forced drafting to do AI work, general sense of disruption at work, low moarale, and almost zero productivity across teams, plus multiple reorgs) I started to look around, on the market, a few weeks before the 20 May layoffs. I figured I have a 50% chance of being let go.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I did not get laid off, but I got offers from startups, and one from a high-growth AI startup I like, and also an offer from Google.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Now, the pros to staying a Meta:</span></p><ul style="margin-left: 20px;margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Context, relationships</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Scale that few others have</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Big Tech perks, relatively “chill” WLB in terms of oncall</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>High TC</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The cons:</span></p><ul style="margin-left: 20px;margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Terrible morale, hard to “move” work through mostly unmotivated teams all around me</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Re-orgs continue, I have very low confidence in middle management (Directors, VPs) to navigate this churn</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Further layoffs are likely: it’s clear that there’s more bloat, surely Zuck will do another round in 2027. And no one is safe during a layoff</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>A ‘doom loop’ for anyone who stays</span></strong><span>: low morale → unmoitivated bith highly compensated engineers → a bloated organization that moves slow”</span></p></li></ul></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>After a new reorg, this engineer got a supportive manager, who made it clear they would help them thrive inside of Meta. So the engineer rejected both the AI startup’s offer and that of Google, deciding to stay… but only for a month!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The AI startup’s founder spent more time with this engineer, increased the equity in the package significantly, and convinced this engineer that at the startup they </span><em><span>matter </span></em><span>as a person, while at Meta they would be doing soulless work, worrying about the next layoff, probably early 2027.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So this engineer also handed in their resignation. And it all started with the layoffs: the engineer assumed there was a 50% chance of being let go and wanted more career stability!</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Those deciding to not resign: stay for the money?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are engineers staying – at least until the end of the year. Another engineer I talked to decided to quit Meta with morale so low, and start his own thing. Management convinced him to stay until the end of the year, hinting at large equity refreshers being handed out around January, which could be in the $1M+ range for this specific engineer.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>A “mercenary” culture at Meta?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I wonder if Meta made a massive mistake by treating engineers as “commodities” and turning their culture into a “mercenary” one. Between March and June, Meta treated engineers as replaceable commodities that could be thrown out or moved between teams, while stripping them of any autonomy. The reassignments to AI labeling were not explained, nor were managers or individuals asked about preferences: from above, someone said that </span><em><span>Alice</span></em><span> and </span><em><span>Bob</span></em><span>, starting on Monday, are no longer with the team, but are training up Meta AI. Never mind that these were the two most experienced engineers on the team, or that </span><em><span>Bob</span></em><span> was the team’s infra expert, and </span><em><span>Alice</span></em><span> the “fixer” engineer on the team.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And all this damage was done, for what? It was to allow Meta to restart its AI coding model development efforts, and release </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2658ec7e-344b-4e2a-a9e1-cb39f2e8d5dd?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Meta Muse Spark</span></a><span>: an AI model that is currently the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/40429bac-9bd8-4e74-854f-7b40117233ae?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>7th most capable</span></a><span> AI model as per Artificial Intelligence Analysis, tied with Grok 4.5. Credit where it’s due: with this model, Meta is now well ahead of Google’s Gemini in capability.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With the damage done, there is little motivation for anyone to stay at Meta – unless they are on a visa, or if it’s about the money. You can have an OK engineering culture with a team who is mostly interested in making more money than what they would elsewhere: but this is more of a mercenary culture, and companies run by mercenaries are more easily out-executed by teams where people believe in the mission of the company.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>If you work at a company that would love to hire from Meta: now is (still) your opening!</span></strong><span> So go for it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And if you’re at Meta: you are </span><em><span>so</span></em><span> in-demand, outside of the company, at places where engineering is still treated as a profit center. As Ryan Nystrom, currently building AI at Notion, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/28cf2ef7-56b6-410c-aef7-a450032a6565?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>put it:</span></a></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Meta friends: the industry is exhilarating right now. Get out. Go build something. The handcuffs are an illusion.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I’m having the time of my life at Notion. Come, and have fun again.”</span></p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>2. Grok Bot: the “OpenClaw moment” for managed AI agents?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>AI agents are already excellent for coding work, and apps like the Claude Cowork desktop app, the Codex desktop app are </span><em><span>okay </span></em><span>at using your own computer for more complex tasks. For example, a few weeks ago, I asked Claude Cowork to help with my business accounting: log into my bank (Revolut), download statements, match them up against invoices filed, and download missing invoices. Cowork took over my browser and did </span><em><span>some</span></em><span> of this, but in the end, I just took over and finished it manually, because it kept getting confused.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In general, I did not find any tool that could speed up my “mindless administrative work of clicking here then here then there then saving this file, then uploading it…”. Until yesterday, that is, when I tried out Grok Bot, a new tool from SpaceX.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>Now, before I continue: I have zero affiliation with SpaceX or Grok, and if anything, I have quite the reservations about anything named “Grok”, given how one month ago, Grok CLI </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b079fd34-9c17-4d4b-b443-d14663164d1d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>uploaded sensitive .env files</span></a><span>, secretly, to the cloud. I’m talking about this tool because the UX it has invented works better than anything before, and I expect many more tools to follow this UX pattern and gain rapid adoption.</span></em></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>OpenClaw, but without needing to set up anything</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The interface of Grok Bot is familiar to all of the other GUI-based AI harnesses (like Codex / ChatGPT, Claude Cowork). </span></strong><span>By doing so, you’re allowing the agent full access to potentially sensitive information and accounts. Could the agent be tricked into giving out your sensitive credentials (like the session token) by a malicious website? Who knows, but probably so!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, we’re stuck in this world where, when APIs with granular control and more secure access do not support certain things, you don’t have much choice but to automate a web-based workflow rather than end-to-end automation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In my case, I took a calculated risk, signed in the bot to my support and contact email, and the agent now took over to do work that would have been impossible via API. And it found emails in spam that were mislabelled.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This felt magical!</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Automating “grunt” workflows</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Another weekly workflow has to do with archiving my podcast recordings. My video production team prepares a several GB-large file with several videos, on their Dropbox account. I want to save this to our team Dropbox account. The flow is this:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>I get a Slack message with a Dropbox link for the podcast video assets</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>I open it, click “copy to Dropbox”</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Once it’s copied to Dropbox, it’s copied to the wrong place: by default it chooses my personal Dropbox.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>I move the files to the team folder, into a specific structure with numbering, by the year published, etc</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>This whole thing takes about 2-3 minutes… but I have to do it every week!</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I automated this whole process in a matter of a few minutes by describing the above workflow to Grok Bot.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>First, I asked it to set up connectors by connecting to Slack and Dropbox. (This is meta, but it’s pretty amazing that with an “AI-native” tool like this you can ask the tool to do stuff in its own app, so you don’t even need to learn yet another new UI!)</span></p><div style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In a matter of minutes, I had my workflow to block and block PR-like emails set up, and set up to run three times a week. This is how </span><em><span>easy</span></em><span> this should be – and it was the first tool where I felt that the tool doesn’t get in the way of helping automate my workflow: instead, it helps with it.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Verbal expression >> UI connectors for casual workflows</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One reason no-code and “visual coding” tools never got mainstream adoption is that they become difficult to manage when you do anything moderately complex. They also take effort to learn, and have a bunch of limitations that you only discover as you go.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In contrast, a lot of the “everyday” work can be described with a few sentences. For example, this spam filtering and blocking exercise is a sentence: even if we could build a massive state machine to get a similar result!</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Grok Bot has lots of issues, but it shows where “general agents” are heading</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Grok bot it not without its flaws. The biggest ones are:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Permissions system is nonexistent. </span></strong><span>There’s a very basic permissions systems with the plugins/connectors, but nothing similar to how Codex or Claude Code asks for permissions before doing any kinds of operations.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Security. </span></strong><span>How secure is this setup? How easy is it for webpages to trick the AI to give out sensitive secrets, keys, session tokens it has? I don’t know: and I assume there are lots of risks here.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Auditing</span></strong><span>. There’s no easy way to review what the agent has done: especially around what “user actions” it did (e.g. send an email, initiate a payment, and so on)</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Privacy: </span></strong><span>how can I block the bot from accessing very sensitive data like passwords, credit card numbers, 2FA restore codes? There currently seems to be no way of doing so.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Transparency:</span></strong><span> what if the developer sneaks malicious code into Grok Bot, how would I or anyone else know? What if they make an update that starts uploading all my private files to their cloud, like Grok CLI did? Also no answer.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Until all the above are solved, Grok Bot is unlikely to be secure enough for enterprise usage. However, the UX and workflow paradigm this tool built is a massive step up from existing tools, and I expect vendors like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google to copy this approach and offer similar harnesses, perhaps with better security / auditing / transparency promises.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the meantime, I’d suggest using Grok Bot at your own risk, and connect it to systems that do not have overly sensitive data stored in them.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>The kind of “general AI harnesses” that will go mainstream will be similar to Grok Bot – I’m pretty certain of this. </span></strong><span>This kind of UX is so intuitive, and the models have gotten good enough to interpret vague instructions. I’m sure there will be a need for more specialized harnesses with more sophisticated UI, but for broadly general administrative and general knowledge work, this kind of user experience works amazingly well.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><em><span>Do leave a comment if you’ve tried out this tool, or another similar one, and what part of your daily workflow it’s made easier.</span></em></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;margin-bottom: 16px;overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>This post is only for paying subscribers of </em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzbGV0dGVyLnByYWdtYXRpY2VuZ2luZWVyLmNvbT91dG1fY2FtcGFpZ249ZW1haWwtaG9tZSZyPTM2eGwxbyIsInAiOjIxMTIwMjE0OSwicyI6NDU4NzA5LCJmIjpmYWxzZSwidSI6MTkzMDQzMTQ4LCJpYXQiOjE3ODY3MjY4NTksImV4cCI6MjEwMjMwMjg1OSwiaXNzIjoicHViLTAiLCJzdWIiOiJsaW5rLXJlZGlyZWN0In0.IVnL2Fpd3o8fuuFkkPkfkHJhGjTXut55UiC-OKHBRGU?" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Pragmatic Engineer</a><em>. item.title: Landing The Plane
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Landing The Plane

James Stanier

“If starting a project is like takeoff, finishing it is like landing, demanding a completely different kind of skill and attention, and it’s where most of the risk accrues. After all, the hardest part of flying a plane is landing it. This article is about why endings are so hard, what goes wrong when you don’t manage them deliberately, and how to land your projects well.”

#Management Productivity
item.description: Landing The Plane

item.title: The Same Side Of The Table
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Same Side Of The Table

“The cardinal rule of meetings with your direct reports is that you are always on the same side of the table. From the moment you walk in to the moment you leave, every single thing that your team does is a reflection and extension of you.”

#Leadership Management
item.description: The Same Side Of The Table

item.title: Advice So Common You Think You Can Skip It
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Advice So Common You Think You Can Skip It

Steve Huynh

“There is a whole class of advice that gets repeated so often it stops registering with us. Somewhere along the way, we decide that anything this common must be for beginners, so we’re allowed to skip it. We nod, we say “Yeah, yeah, yeah,” and then we go looking for the real advice. You can spot this sort of advice by noticing (a) how fast you agree with it and (b) how rarely you do it.”

#CareerGrowth
item.description: Advice So Common You Think You Can Skip It

item.title: Control And Complexity: Tension In Systems Design
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Control And Complexity: Tension In Systems Design

Fred Hebert

“The adoption of LLMs in software development has led countless organizations to rapidly change their practices and structures. Old methods are questioned, replaced, and repurposed as the economics around creating new code get shaken up. Because humans and LLMs aren’t interchangeable, the dynamics in play are also very different. Systems are systems, and so regardless of what is changing, there are known patterns on which we can draw to provide some guidance and warnings.”

#Architecture AI
item.description: Control And Complexity: Tension In Systems Design

item.title: A Harness For Every Task: Dynamic Workflows In Claude Code
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
A Harness For Every Task: Dynamic Workflows In Claude Code

Thariq Shihipar

“Workflows allow you to dynamically create harnesses that enable Claude to solve all of those problems and more natively inside of Claude Code. You can also share and re-use these workflows with others. In this article, I’ll cover my initial workflows experiences and learnings so you can take full advantage.”

#AI Guide DevEx
item.description: A Harness For Every Task: Dynamic Workflows In Claude Code

item.title: Software Engineering At A Proprietary Trading Company: Optiver
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Software Engineering At A Proprietary Trading Company: Optiver

Gergely Orosz

“Building better AI models getting more focus than lower latency, owning the full stack from applications to building custom hardware, very different incentives to most tech companies in play, and more.”

#DeepDive IndustryTrends
item.description: Software Engineering At A Proprietary Trading Company: Optiver

item.title: Write For People
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Write For People

Vicki Boykis

“We should strive for simplicity. If we can’t, it could be because we don’t understand the problem ourselves yet enough to compress it. That’s cool. Understanding things is hard. Naming things is hard, for the same reason. But it should be a little harder. Like 10% harder. We should be more tired than the model, or at least a little less verbose.”

#AI Communication
item.description: Write For People

break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><span>In a service-based architecture, a single product screen showing a user profile, that user’s five most recent orders, the delivery status of each order, and a short list of recommendations requires data from four separate services. Each service stores only its own data, so none of the four services returns the full set on its own. In other words, the caller issues four separate calls, and merges the resulting four responses in the structure needed for the user interface. This merging step is API composition, and it exists in every system where data is split across more than one service.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The code that performs this merging can run in several places. It can run inside the mobile application, on a server in the datacenter, at a CDN edge location, or inside one of the four services. Putting a server between the mobile application and the four services adds a network hop, which sounds like it should cost extra time. However, it usually reduces total load time instead, because a round trip between a phone and a server on a weak mobile connection can take a few hundred milliseconds, while a round trip between two services inside the same datacenter takes a fraction of a millisecond. To put it simply, trading four expensive round trips for one expensive round trip plus four cheap ones is often a large net saving.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, latency is only the first tradeoff. The place where the merge operation runs also determines what happens when one of the four services is unavailable, how much of the response can be cached, and which team has to approve a change before the screen ships.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we are going to dive deep into the area of the API composition problem and the patterns associated with it. This take is from one of my favorite voices in software reliability and observability: Charity Majors, CTO and cofounder of Honeycomb, co-author of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/210bc125-edd4-4411-8e31-544e55064ae8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Observability Engineering</span></a><span>. (Note: the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/210bc125-edd4-4411-8e31-544e55064ae8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>second edition of Observability Engineering</span></a><span> is out, and it’s pretty much a full rewrite of the book, I recommend grabbing it if you’re building reliable systems)</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this episode, I sat down with Charity to discuss how her thinking on AI has evolved, why she believes it is becoming a foundational part of software engineering, and what that means for how teams build, review, and ship software.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We explore how AI is changing the economics of code generation, why reliability and verification are increasingly the bottlenecks, and why the rise of non-deterministic systems requires more engineering discipline. Charity shares her views on code reviews, observability, DevOps, leadership, and why both AI skeptics and enthusiasts are getting important things right.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);">Takeaways from the conversation with Charity</h3><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/cf81be0d-0573-4bdc-a878-6ed2d8b91fe4?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/HC8T1OlgYi0" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Here are 13 parts I found especially interesting, talking with Charity:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>1. In March 2025, Charity told the audience at SREcon to try vibe coding, and back then, the response was grumbling.</span></strong><span> Charity’s point was that people who are skeptical of AI should still learn to use it, because you can complain better if you’ve learned it. At this time, Charity still saw AI having a bigger impact than a new programming language, but was skeptical that it would have a generational impact.​</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>2. Charity’s turning point in seeing AI as a generational change was in November 2025. </span></strong><span>This was due to Opus 4.5, but Charity argues that the coding harness (Claude Code) made the bigger difference. Because thanks to Claude Code, harnesses went from being more of a shell script to serious infrastructure.​</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>3. The impact of AI on the industry in 2025 was similar to the impact of the cloud in 2010. </span></strong><span>Looking back, Charity is comfortable saying this: in 2010, it became clear that cloud computing was certainly going mainstream and would change the infra-layer. After 2025, it’s also clear that AI will have a similar impact on the infrastructure of building software.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>4. Engineers who were skeptical of AI up to 2025: they had good reason to be so.</span></strong><span> This was because we’ve seen plenty of technologies and innovations in the past that all promised to transform the software industry, but later fell short. Examples include COBOL (a technology promising that programmers would no longer be needed to create software), neural nets, no-code and low-code tools.​</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>5. The question engineers need to answer: what would it take for you to be fully comfortable shipping code you have not read? </span></strong><span>Charity believes it is a “when” and not an “if” that professional software engineers will ship code they never looked at – and thus do not understand – to production. Engineering is building the systems that validate this code, and allow shipping with full confidence.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>6. AI could have the software industry go through the “pets” to “cattle” change that compute infra went through in the 2010s. </span></strong><span>Up to now, writing software from scratch was far more expensive than editing existing software. But now, generating hundreds of variants of a function can be done faster than how long it would take you to hand-write it once.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Charity believes that we might be at the beginning of the transition from “pets” to “cattle” that happened at the hardware infrastructure layer. Before the 2010s, configuring and repairing individual servers was commonly done. But with tools like Terraform and Kubernetes, individual servers having issues are no longer fixed up: they are re-created instead. Charity thinks the same might happen with code, sooner rather than later. When there’s an issue with the code, generate new code that solves it, and is verifyably correct.​</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>7. Her contrarian take: code review is overrated, and the least valuable part of what humans add to software engineering. </span></strong><span>Charity says that humans are good at conversations and deciding what to build, not reading code to check for correctness, syntax and bugs.​</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>8. Charity’s verdict of 20 years of DevOps: it failed. </span></strong><span>The DevOps feedback was about trying to create a feedback loop that connected people writing the code to the code running in production. She thinks that the “ops people: learn to code!” wave worked, but the “software engineers: understand your code in production” failed,  to this day.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>9. Non-deterministic systems require more engineering discipline versus before. </span></strong><span>With code written by AI, we’re reducing the trust in the code (because we no longer wrote it), so we need to increase trust at the other part of the development process. Specifically, at validation: with things like tests, evals, and conformance testing.​</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>10. Charity’s career advice for engineering directors: run towards the waves, and get AI on your resume, immediately. </span></strong><span>It’s an anxious time to work in tech, thanks to all the change, driven by AI. Charity reminds us that anxiety and excitement are physiologically almost the same, but the difference is agency. When you have no agency, you’re more likely to get anxious, and when you do, you’re more likely to get excited.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So her advice to anxious engineering directors: consider going back to IC work, where you’ll have far more agency. IC work is well-respected, getting back to it has never been easier, but the window to do so is closing. As she put it:​</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“The next time you’ll have a job interview, you’ll be filtered out if you don’t have AI experience.”​</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>11. On AI fatigue: take back control with small acts! </span></strong><span>We talked about various types of AI fatigue: reviewing AI slop, getting tired of the AI hype, and getting worn down by “doom trolling” by AI CEOs. Charity finds small acts of taking control back in your work from AI tools help. For example, none of the Honeycomb team uses AI on Wednesdays.​</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>12. Charity would like to see both the “AI-pilled” and the “anti-AI” camps tell the stories better. </span></strong><span>As she put it:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“There are some really incredible things happening in software right now, for example, with rewrites and with automating away toil. Not a single person that I’ve talked to would give up using AI.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But half of the people are seeing the </span><em><span>wins,</span></em><span> and they’re not connecting it to the </span><em><span>cost</span></em><span>, which makes them think that their coworkers are just afraid of getting automated out of existence.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So that’s my beg to everyone who listens to this: tell the whole story! Talk about the costs as well. We’re all in it together.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>13. Charity’s rule on AI writing: do not send any message/email to a human that you yourself have not read in full. </span></strong><span>She also says that it would take them longer to read whatever you send than it took you to produce it: it’s probably slop!</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Orchestration</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>GitHub made a specific choice about where the value sits.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Rather than building its own model and competing on raw generation, it built a control layer that coordinates many agents and keeps their work governed, all inside the pull request workflow that developers use every day.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The mechanics start with where the code runs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>GitHub’s coding agent operates in its own ephemeral development environment, which is a temporary workspace that exists only for that task. It is powered by GitHub Actions, the same automation system that runs tests and builds on the platform [1][2]. In practice, you assign a task to the agent the way you would open a ticket. The agent reads through the repository, edits files, runs the tests and linters (tools that check code for problems), and opens a draft pull request for a person to review [1]. Each cloud run happens in a fully isolated, single-use Linux environment hosted by GitHub. Every new task starts from a clean workspace [4]. The review step stays human, which keeps the existing quality gate intact.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" are already accustomed to handling issues and pull requests, this design adds agents to a pretty familiar workflow. Reviewing a colleague’s branch is not so different from reviewing an agent’s branch.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Routing to other companies’ models is a deliberate decision. GitHub is positioning the workflow, the execution environment, and the governance layer as the durable product, and treating the underlying model as a swappable component.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let us now look at how Vercel developed its architecture around what happens after the code exists. This is somewhere between a working demo and production-ready software.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Production</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Vercel starts from a different premise where code generation is assumed, and the design deals with carrying the generated code into production. This is the stage where most enterprise software work actually happens, because it involves existing applications rather than fresh prototypes.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The rebuilt version of v0, Vercel’s generation product, runs on a sandbox. It is an isolated space for executing code that imports a real GitHub repository and automatically pulls in the project’s environment variables and configuration. Every prompt produces code that fits the actual application and lives in the repository itself [5].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A Git panel handles the workflow around it. You create a branch for each chat, open a pull request against the main branch, and deploy when it merges. This means a product manager or a designer can ship through the same review process an engineer uses [5].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Vercel’s rationale about this approach is that AI-assisted building is already happening inside companies, and it has produced real failures. Incidents have been reported, such as credentials pasted into prompts, private data reaching the public internet, and deleted databases, often with the audit trail left empty [5]. Therefore, wrapping code generation in real deployment controls is the right response.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table workflow is the execution layer. Every sandbox runs inside a Firecracker microVM, a lightweight virtual machine that isolates untrusted code. The reason for this isolation is that the code an AI wrote is code you have yet to review. Therefore, running it needs a boundary strong enough to contain mistakes. A microVM provides that strong boundary.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The billing model depends on how agents actually run. Vercel’s Fluid compute lets several requests share one running instance, with one using the processor while another waits on input or output. It charges for active processor time while treating wait time as free [6][7]. Agentic workloads spend much of their time waiting on a model to respond, so this pricing matches the real work being done.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: with a frustration many developers face in their careers. The thing that worked in a demo behaves differently in production. However, Vercel’s design tries to close that gap by making the preview a real deployment from the start.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Nevertheless, strong isolation carries a cost per unit of compute. There is an open question about whether the heaviest workloads eventually move to cheaper execution options elsewhere. Vercel’s wager is that a single, convenient platform keeps them in place.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To summarize, GitHub owns the workflow, and Vercel owns the route to production. Both of them still depend on one assumption that Replit chose to attack directly. Let us look at that now.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Verification</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Replit concentrated its work on whether autonomously generated code genuinely works using a verification loop built into the agent itself.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Replit’s Agent 3 runs what the company calls a reflection loop. The agent generates code, runs it, tests the result, and repairs failures, repeating that cycle until the tests pass [8]. This loop is reliable because of how the testing is done. Replit built a REPL-based verification system that runs code immediately and pairs that execution with a real browser it drives automatically, so it can click buttons, submit forms, and check data the way a user would [9].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The specific problem this approach targets has a memorable name inside Replit: the Potemkin interface. It is basically a feature that looks complete on screen yet fails the moment it is used [9]. Catching that class of error is what allows the agent to run on its own for more than 200 minutes at a stretch, a large increase over the roughly 20 minutes of its predecessor [8][9].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The verification runs as its own process.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A testing subagent follows a simple cycle of taking an action, observing the result, and repeating. When it finishes, it returns a summary to the main agent describing what works and what broke [9]. This multi-hundred-step testing costs a median of roughly twenty cents per session and runs several times faster and more cheaply than relying on general-purpose computer-use models [9].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: shipped a feature that looked finished and later broke understands the problem here. Replit is trying to automate the check that catches exactly that, so that the automation can be trusted.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A verification loop reduces the risk substantially. Some failures still surface only under conditions a single test session might miss, which keeps this a pretty hard problem even with a capable tester in place.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Interoperability</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Every architecture we have looked at assumes its agent can reach tools and data that live outside the model, and doing that cleanly requires a common method. That method is the Model Context Protocol, usually shortened to MCP.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Before a standard like this existed, connecting several AI applications to several external tools meant writing a separate custom integration for each pairing. In this approach, the number of integrations grew quickly as both sides multiplied. Anthropic introduced MCP to replace those fragmented, one-off connections with a single protocol, so each application and each tool implements the standard once and then works with everything else without additional changes [10].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A host, which is the AI application such as an IDE or a chat client, creates one or more clients, and each client connects to a server that exposes some capability [11]. A server offers three kinds of capability:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Tools, which the model can call to take an action, such as creating a record or running a query.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Resources, which supply context data the model can read, such as a file or a database schema.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Prompts, which provide reusable instruction templates.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The whole exchange runs over a defined message format across either a local or a remote connection. The effect is that a tool provider builds one MCP server and every compliant agent can use it [11].</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Replit was among the earliest developer tools to integrate MCP [10], GitHub added an MCP registry to VS Code where a server can be enabled with a single click [3], and Stripe runs an official MCP server for its payment operations [12].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Going deeper, MCP also standardizes how agents reach existing APIs rather than replacing those APIs. A single shared entry point also concentrates security in one place. That makes careful control over which servers an agent may use an important part of any real deployment.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Tradeoffs</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Each of these architectures and approaches has trade-offs:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>GitHub gains breadth and governance by routing to many vendors’ models. But the cost is that it owns the surface rather than the intelligence underneath. Whether a coordination and governance layer stays valuable as models and agents keep changing is an open question.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Vercel gains strong isolation by running generated code inside microVMs, and that isolation carries a cost per unit of compute. There is a question about whether the heaviest workloads eventually move to cheaper execution elsewhere</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Replit gains long stretches of autonomy through its verification loop, and the more work an agent does on its own, the more weight rests on that verification being right. The Potemkin problem (code that looks complete yet fails when used) stays difficult even with a capable tester, because some failures appear only in situations a test session might miss.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>MCP gains a clean, reusable way to connect agents and tools, and a shared standard also concentrates risk into a common entry point. When many agents reach many tools through one protocol, controlling which servers an agent may use, and their permission levels, becomes a central problem rather than a detail.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Understanding these costs is what separates picking one of these tools from understanding why it was built the way it was.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The pattern across all three companies is the same. Code generation became cheap, so the value moved into the engineering that surrounds it. Each company placed its bet on a different piece of that surrounding work.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>GitHub bet on orchestration, building a control layer that runs and governs many agents inside the pull request workflow developers already use.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Vercel bet on production, wrapping generated code in real deployments and running it inside isolated microVMs built for untrusted code.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Lastly, Replit bet on verification, driving a real browser in a self-testing loop so an agent can work on its own for hours and still be checked.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Underneath all three, MCP provides the common protocol that lets any agent reach any tool, which is why every one of these platforms now supports it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>References:</span></strong></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;margin-bottom: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height:
