break-word;font-family: 'SF Pro Display', -apple-system, system-ui, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Inter', 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif, 'Apple Color Emoji', 'Segoe UI Emoji', 'Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: 400;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em><span>Before we start: I’ll be in New York, on 15 September, presenting the keynote at </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0113e98e-31a6-4935-aa3b-ea7987479664?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>LDX3 New York</span></a><span>, doing a book signing, and hanging out with attendees. The focus of the conference is engineering leadership at a time when things are moving very fast. </span><strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0113e98e-31a6-4935-aa3b-ea7987479664?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>See the full agenda and get tickets</span></a><span>. </span></strong><span>If you’ll be around – hopefully catch you there!</span></em></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>The Pragmatic Engineer is back from our summer break. We resume with a detailed deepdive about the trading industry, and interesting engineering challenges that come when working at a company that has no external customers, but where a single, unfortunate enough software bug could wipe out the whole company.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In tech recruitment, proprietary trading companies have a particularly high bar and typically offer compensation on a par with, or even exceeding, Big Tech; right at the top of the market. That’s because for these market makers, success is all about gaining a competitive edge over rivals. Such competitive advantages today includes software that is superior to that at their competitors.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Software engineers tend to know little about trading companies – and this piece aims to change that. </span></strong><span>Trading companies build bespoke hardware stacks and have larger platform engineering teams than most workplaces. For software engineers, it’s a lucrative niche in terms of compensation, full-stack (hardware to software) work and for engineering challenges, and so we decided to go deeper in this interesting area.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In order to find out more, The Pragmatic Engineer sat down with a leading proprietary trading firm, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a54337e3-640a-47cd-8526-f959513cac8f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Optiver</span></a><span>. Headquartered in Amsterdam, they also have a large engineering presence in the US and globally. We met engineers and engineering leaders to learn in depth how engineering works in a modern trading business, with contributions from:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c5e67c46-5517-4dd1-9ead-ff64ba7a9b4e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Alex Itkin</span></a><span>: CTO, Optiver US</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/aa3ffade-82e8-4ac1-a18e-b017e2ad5188?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Pat Cooney</span></a><span>: Head of Global Platform Engineering</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/607c5eba-d150-4733-8ebd-e74ff95f3445?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>David Gross</span></a><span>: Technology Lead, Options</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Thanks to everyone at Optiver for taking part in this report which lifts the lid on how software engineering is done when even nanoseconds can count. In this article, we look into a software engineering environment that’s distinct from what you expect at most startups and Big Tech. For example:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>No external customers. </span></strong><span>Usually, companies have consumer customers (B2C), business customers (B2B), or both. But not trading houses like Optiver, where their own business is </span><em><span>the</span></em><span> customer. This is a different reality: there’s no external deadlines and related pressures, but personal motivation to improve is highly valued.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Latency: “enemy number one”. </span></strong><span>Nearly every major engineering decision at Optiver is made in the interest of minimizing latency – the amount of time between a request and response. This approach is present across the software stack and in kernel-level work. It’s why Optiver manufactures its own hardware.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Today, latency is the floor, and AI models are becoming a differentiator. </span></strong><span>Gone are the days of having lower latency than the competition allowing for arbitrage opportunities to make risk-free profits. Prices were shared on reels of ticker tape and printed in newspapers. Investors contacted brokers to place orders.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>First wave of electronification (early/mid 1990s).</span></strong><span> Financial markets moved onto computer screens but orders were still entered manually.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Automated trading (late 1990s to ~2015).</span></strong><span> Computers did the same as human traders, but faster and at scale. 1);"><span>High-Frequency Trading (HFT)</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>High-frequency trading involves placing high volumes of orders at lightning speed in an effort to take advantage of extremely rapid market movements. In this domain, speed is the biggest advantage, and achieving it obviously involves high-performance computing. The basic trading loop is run millions of times a day. It’s made up of three steps:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Watch</span></strong><span> the market for new information like price changes</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Decide</span></strong><span> what the information means and the right trade to make</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Send</span></strong><span> a trade to the exchange before competitors do</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In trading, timing is everything, and for some types of trade even nanoseconds count. Optiver’s fastest trading system operates in the realm of sub-nanosecond, where measurement noise becomes a challenge in itself. Software, hardware, and physics are all involved, along with microwave and shortwave links between data centers, and custom-manufactured chips.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>We go deep into this in the “Hardware Engineering” section below.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>However, in this niche, even ultra-low latency is no longer a competitive moat in itself</span></strong><span>. As competitors have squeezed performance out of their systems, focus has shifted towards fine-tuning of trading strategies. Today, Optiver invests substantially more in building better models than it does in lowering latencies.</span><em><span> More on this in the “Network and physical infrastructure” </span></em><span>section below.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>HFT evolves faster than other industries. </span></strong><span>Profitable strategies don’t last long, opportunities are fleeting, and innovation is a constant. In this environment, a tool like AI is relatively straightforward to implement because trading houses like Optiver are well used to change in their daily business environment. </span><em><span>More on this topic in the ‘Optiver & AI’ section.</span></em></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Plenty of ML & math</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There’s a big role for machine learning (ML) and mathematics in quantitative trading. A good chunk of Optiver’s business is the buying and selling of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4f7a446d-b8be-430d-b2c8-d341b88d2c28?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>options</span></a><span>, and the pricing of these rests on mathematical theorems like the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/81712d80-043b-4ed5-90e0-431af2ccb4c1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Black-Scholes model</span></a><span>. Traders, quants, and even software engineers building option-pricing strategies must understand the math of this problem space.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Over time, machine learning is becoming more important than math models, but it’s worth keeping in mind that trading is not purely an ML pursuit.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>AI infra providers are heavily involved. </span></strong><span>NVIDIA, Groq, and Cerebras are actively courting trading firms, due to how much money they spend on GPUs. For example, see Hudson River Trading </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e6a8dc2a-18e5-42dc-8493-94019adaaf57?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>discussing</span></a><span> Blackwell deployments at NVIDIA’s GTC conference, or Jump Trading being among the first </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fa72aacd-b1a5-4161-ab5f-fa8a2df5208f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>to deploy</span></a><span> next-gen Vera Rubin systems. HFT companies have very clear monetization paths for GPUs and spend large sums on hardware, hence why NVIDIA and other suppliers are keen to partner with them.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>AI labs poach trading talent</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One new trend is AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI recruiting from prop shops, defying the assumption that AI labs mostly recruit from Big Tech. There are a few reasons why AI labs seek out talent from the trading world:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Infra expertise.</span></strong><span> Prop shops like Optiver have spent decades operating their own data centers and deploying on-prem hardware at co-location facilities.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Custom, high-performance hardware. </span></strong><span>Prop shops also often build their own hardware and their kernel stacks achieve very low latencies. That’s a talent AI labs seek!</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Skillsets. </span></strong><span>The highest-paying destinations for CS majors out of standout colleges are often prop shops, paying top-of-market compensation for standout talent. </span><em><span>Outside of select colleges prop shops recruit from, however, there tends to be little awareness about these companies for new grads, or across the industry.</span></em></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>2. Engineering organization</span></h2><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Two eras of Optiver tech</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver’s history can be seen as two distinct ages:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Regional systems (“unblock yourself”: 1986-2020):</span></strong><span> internal systems and platforms were built to serve local needs, such as building support for a market. Systems built exclusively for the US, Europe, or Asia were common.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Global platforms (“build for the whole company”: 2020-present): </span></strong><span>Optiver recently started to build new systems to work globally across their platform. This global focus is also why the company is investing a lot more in its platform engineering arm. A globalization push started around 2023, and its momentum has been growing.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The benefit of the old “unblock yourself” approach of local teams building whatever they needed, was that it enabled them to move fast and not get held up by dependencies. But this became problematic because of fragmentation and duplication, and the downsides became more visible over time:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Fragmentation: different teams use different technologies, frameworks, and infrastructure</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Duplication: teams in different parts of the business independently build the same or very similar services</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The career trajectory of Pat Cooney, Optiver’s head of platform engineering, mirrors the shift to a global platform: he was the CTO of Optiver in Europe in the mid-2010s when the business was split by region, and was appointed head of platform engineering in 2025 when that approach was replaced.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver’s approach to continuous integration (CI) has also evolved. Previously, the company had several regional CI services, but from 2025, it started to rebuild its CI system with two new goals:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Build for scale: </span></strong><span>create a CI system built to scale across regions and stand the test of time</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Use from any region: </span></strong><span>standardize deployment pipelines, so that code built in one location can run anywhere without friction</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>How roles work together</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At Optiver, there are three main areas for tech roles:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Engineering</span></strong><span>: build and own the full trading-platform stack</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Research</span></strong><span>: quantitative scientists who build models and predictive signals to create and improve trading algorithms. Typically, their background is in math, physics, economics, and statistics</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Trading</span></strong><span>: quantitative traders who watch live markets, adjust trading system parameters in response to conditions, and build tools to automate decisions</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>In reality, the boundaries between these areas are porous. </span></strong><span>Yes, people do the job they were hired for, but it’s common to also see researchers roll up their sleeves and take part in implementing a trading strategy, or software engineers conducting research.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: task</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Cross-functional collaboration between roles is very common. </span></strong><span>For example, when developing market signals and associated trading strategies, it’s normal for engineers, researchers, and traders to collaborate on most, if not all, projects.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>End-to-end ownership, plus autonomy, is a given. </span></strong><span>Engineers have autonomy in how they get things done, and they own and solve problems from the ideas stage through to implementation. There is a limited amount of guidance for trading, and it’s down to engineers to find the right solution.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In many ways, this approach to software engineering is pretty similar to startups’: software engineers get limited guidance and lots of autonomy. In order to succeed at tech startups, engineers typically need to understand the business, as well as being excellent at building production-ready software. It’s the same at Optiver, where understanding the business means understanding markets.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Platform engineering</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Before Optiver’s globalized platform efforts started seriously in ~2023, regions duplicated effort:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Multiple implementations of identical core logic</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Each region had its own systems, frameworks, and infrastructure</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Local teams built whatever they needed in an “unblock yourself” culture</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But that’s all changed. An obvious sign of global platform efforts is the appointment of Optiver’s first global CTO, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/78a3c513-f922-4e8c-b082-d1185df2754b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Lance Braunstein</span></a><span>, who joined with a mandate to scale the platform.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Roughly 30-40% of Optiver’s 950 engineers work on the platform. </span></strong><span>In contrast, a more typical ratio at other large tech companies is for 15-20% of engineers to be dedicated to platform work.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Prior to the global platform, there was a lot more tolerance of development experience friction; new engineers could spend weeks checking out the codebase and getting their build system to work. This mindset has changed, with the platform team stressing user empathy and reducing friction on engineers’ journeys, like by setting up build pipelines for their software.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Now, the platform is beginning to reimagine itself as built for AI.</span></strong><span> As agents proliferate at Optiver, users are both humans and automated systems. The goal of this shift is to empower people to decompose work into workstreams and orchestrate agents. Two projects were launched earlier this year by the platform team for agentic work:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>AI gateway</span></strong><span>: gives Optiver engineers access to models</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ba0ba164-bef8-4fba-9df6-419d3c70fbd1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>MCP</span></a><span> hosting platform:</span></strong><span> makes it easy for engineers to access internal systems and tools via agents</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>How trading teams are organized</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Trading teams at Optiver have three roles:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Traders decide strategy and make risk decisions</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Researchers and quantitative analysts (“quants”) build hypotheses, pricing models, and run evaluations</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Engineers build production systems</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In practice, these roles overlap. This was true before the AI era, but it seems to be accelerating with AI adoption. Most traders and quants have STEM backgrounds without recent production coding experience. AI enables quantitatively-minded people to automate workflows with agents and to implement strategies.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Trading teams are organized by asset class and strategy.</span></strong><span> For example (asset classes in </span><em><span>italic</span></em><span>):</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A large team is focused on a broad area like </span><em><span>options</span></em></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A team focused on </span><em><span>cash markets</span></em><span> and building strategies for exchange-traded funds (ETF) and stocks.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A team focused on machine learning (ML) and trading in the </span><em><span>cash market</span></em><span>.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Within larger teams, there are horizontal and vertical sub-teams. </span></strong><span>Horizontal teams take on challenges that impact any trading desk; for example, pricing is a horizontal team as the underlying mechanism is the same whether a soybean or an index fund being priced.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Vertical teams are similar to “tiger teams”, accelerators, and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/27f55e3d-e685-45cd-af9e-13afd93ec238?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>program teams</span></a><span> at other companies. They focus on short-term goals attached to a few different desks in a location like the US, Amsterdam, Mumbai or Sydney.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Each team has a trading or research lead and a tech lead, who identify work for the team to do. The overall direction is set by a partnership structure, similar to an investment bank, but partners are not necessarily in charge of teams. At Optiver, partners are collections of senior people responsible for overall strategy.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Regardless of asset class or vertical, every trading team builds a version of a trading loop with four components.</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Retrieval of market-related information</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Collecting signals to work 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Execution of strategies (sending orders to market)</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver runs on an ownership culture, with the principle that the best engineers take work personally and care deeply about Optiver’s systems, decisions, and outcomes. There is no notion of throwing work over the wall to a QA team.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver’s ownership model:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Traders and engineers define problems together.</span></strong><span> Engineers design, build, test, deploy, and monitor a solution. There are hundreds of production changes daily</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Design reviews for architectural decision-making.</span></strong><span> When an engineer has a project that entails architectural change to the stack, the engineer is responsible for bringing multiple options with the pros and cons to the team for consultation. The goal is to share information and knowledge, and to make decisions</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver pushes new hires and interns to develop ownership. From day one, engineers have something they own and are assigned a real project with mentoring support. Production code changes are an expectation for new hires. Within a year, a new hire becomes the experienced person in their domain, ramping up the next engineer. This is explicitly emphasized in Optiver’s onboarding materials:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Case study: the Options Org</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver started life with options trading. The word ‘Optiver’ is actually a Dutch portmanteau of “options” and “trader”, so it’s unsurprising that the options team is among the most developed parts of the operation, with engineers split across multiple locations. The organization is composed of both vertical and horizontal teams.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One of the technical systems for which the Options organization is responsible is the retreat system. When Optiver trades an option, that trade itself changes the price of the next quote on offer. The retreat system has to reprice the entire option surface (i.e., all options related to the one just traded). This is called a ‘retreat’.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the case of S&P options, the option surface can consist of thousands of options that have to be updated. Ten years ago, the retreat process took seconds; now, through optimizations at every level of the stack, it’s down to nanoseconds.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" occurs: the original quote is stale and a trader needs to remove the bid from the exchange before anyone can exploit it. Faster firms can take advantage of others’ stale prices, leading to an adversarial market dynamic.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Horizontal vs vertical team structures</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Vertical teams work on specific tactical problems related to local trading desks with a focus on immediate impact. But they are not short-term or temporary teams, even if they work on short-term problems. They’re empowered to solve the most important current problems, end-to-end. On the other hand, horizontal teams serve most desks, and have longer time horizons because they work on cross-cutting problems like pricing, market connectivity, or auto-trading.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>3. Software tech stack</span></h2><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Basic trading loop & three-layer tech stack</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Most trading software applications or services (aka “apps”) at Optiver can be simplified to the basic trading loop. Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);"><span>Signals</span></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is the information-gathering phase where services collect market data such as prices and order book information, and also run various data calculations, such as pricing algorithms and machine learning pipelines. These signals are made available to strategy applications/services which decide how to trade.</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);"><span>Strategy</span></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A single trading strategy typically focuses on a particular class of assets and trades, and many different strategies run concurrently. The strategy sets what and how to trade, but doesn’t execute the trade; that’s the next step.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>All strategies are enveloped by a risk management system that can block trades and stop individual strategies. To be effective, it has a broader view of the combined risk level of multiple strategies.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Risk mechanisms can include human oversight, with traders tweaking strategy parameters, and also automated monitoring that checks if apps are outputting orders within expected parameters, regardless of what the algorithm wants. The latter approach is essential in low latency strategies where faster-than-human reaction speeds are needed.</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);"><span>Execution</span></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The execution step involves executing trades on exchanges. There’s a hard ‘separation of concerns’ principle where execution steps are only permitted to execute the trade. No additional logic is meant to run there.</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);"><span>Ultra low-latency loop</span></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In some market-making use cases where nanosecond-level latencies matter, much of this process may run within a single chip (FPGA or ASIC) where the strategy part can be </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0dfae088-9027-40a8-94b2-7c83df902f6f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>memoized</span></a><span> with precomputed responses for all expected input patterns. This is then burned into the hardware to minimize latency from when market information arrives until a trading order is issued.</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);"><span>The tech stack’s three layers</span></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>All apps implementing the trading loop sit on top of a multi-layered internal platform:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Basic infrastructure layer</span></strong><span>: the stuff you’d see at most tech companies (CI/CD pipelines, k8s, Kafka, Postgres, etc), but they’re also customizing their stack. They run their own data centers, have custom hardware, custom Linux kernels, customized CI tooling, and databases.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Domain-specific infrastructure</span></strong><span> contains core trading-specific services such as trading data dictionaries, metadata on securities, and the trade booking system.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" Avoiding hand-offs between traders and engineers for reimplementation in C++ saves time, and empowers non-engineers to solve their problems directly, in line with the “unblock yourself” ethos.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Rust</span></strong><span> is starting to play a significant role in research tooling and service orchestration, likely driven by the performance requirements. 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>CI/CD stack</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Much of the software that Optiver builds interacts with custom hardware, custom Linux kernels, and requires predictable compute performance for predictable results in performance tests. These are all constraints that the CI/CD stack has to operate within.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Optiver’s CI/CD runs on bare metal machines, </span></strong><span>with custom hardware installed, the right OS tweaks, and a well-understood performance profile. Interestingly, this means Optiver needs to plan capacity in advance for its CI/CD clusters in the same way as it plans capacity for production systems. This is tricky since AI-coding tools started boosting the number of builds an average engineer does in a day.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>They chose GitHub Actions as their CI Platform for the seamless development experience with GitHub. Unfortunately, Actions doesn’t provide overall, system-level metrics like queue times and utilizations, which are critical information for planning CI cluster capacity. Therefore, they had to build a bespoke observability layer over GitHub Actions pipelines with GitHub webhooks.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Data</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When it comes to databases and storage systems in general, Optiver is a big user of </span><strong><span>Kafka</span></strong><span>, </span><strong><span>Postgres</span></strong><span>, and </span><strong><span>Databricks</span></strong><span> (the company built its entire data platform around this).</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A few interesting details show the role of Postgres:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>They contributed </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4d8ea78e-a693-4ebb-870a-44543bf89b70?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>a new timestamp type</span></a><span> to Postgres, allowing timestamps to be expressed with nanosecond precision. Few Postgres applications care about nanosecond-level precision, and this wasn’t available “out of the box”.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>They built their own internal version of the NOTIFY - LISTEN mechanism called ‘PG Feed,’ based on Postgres’ write-ahead log. This is used for distributing high-fanout, latency-sensitive messages to clients like pricing and configuration data, whereas using something like Kafka may involve additional disk reads and writes, which imply unwanted latency.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver generally picks industry-standard tooling, but heavily tweaks it to fit their specific performance needs. Not many tech companies of this size tweak Postgres or GitHub Actions, let alone Linux kernels!</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>4. Hardware engineering, FPGAs and Silicon</span></h2><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>The hot path</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In high frequency trading, a “hot path” is a sequence of events in a trading application, starting with an external trigger to issue a market order, e.g., a change in price.
