20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;">Memoization pre-computes the decision and risk check (2-3) between events. The trigger time path is match inbound pattern (1) → emit pre-computed response (4)</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Everyone on the market sees the same thing, so being first to react is critical when opportunities arise. </span></strong><span>This is because those opportunities disappear once orders are made, since those orders change the conditions which created an opportunity in the first place</span><strong><span>.</span></strong><span> That’s why Optiver puts so much effort into minimizing hot path latency.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Depending on the different triggers and decisions, there are actually multiple latency-sensitive hot paths, such as:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Quote/requote - continually update prices shared with the market</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Aggress/take (trigger-to-order) - detect an opportunity and execute trade</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Retreat/reprice - After completing an order, reprice</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Cancel/pull - Cancel orders</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Latency progression</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Folks whom we talked with at Optiver say the firm hasn’t yet reached the physical limit of what’s possible. Below are two interesting presentations on this quest for lower latency:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f08026de-f700-48f6-ac96-6847b0826384?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>When a microsecond is an eternity</span></a><span> (2017) by software engineer Carl Cook</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cbb4c1a5-d7dc-402f-95f8-c7783b6b1ef9?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>When nanoseconds matter: </span></a><span>ultrafast trading in C++ (2024) by Optiver tech lead, David Gross</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Custom hardware is a logical step for optimizing latency at a trading firm like Optiver. Moving from microseconds to nanoseconds in latency requires improvements across hot paths. Here are some typical optimization steps:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>A “regular” C++ app.</span></strong><span> A trading application starts life as a regular C++ app that’s optimized until CPU context switching and the kernel’s network stack become the slowest or highest variance parts.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Pin CPU cores.</span></strong><span> To address CPU context switching, engineers at Optiver first pin CPU cores. Operating systems will typically run multiple programs on each CPU core. This means a program can be temporarily stopped and replaced by another program. This is not desirable for consistent high performance, so a CPU core is pinned exclusively to a specific trading program, preventing it from being interrupted by other programs.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Work with the network card, bypassing the kernel. </span></strong><span>To address performance variance in the networking stack, they bypass the kernel and work with the network card directly. Normally, when data arrives from the exchange, the kernel sits between the network card and the application, making networking safe and uniform to program against. This imposes a small “speed tax” (aka, it runs slower) that is well worth it for many applications, but is a cause of lag and performance variance for latency-sensitive use cases like Optiver’s. By taking the kernel out of the data path, they forgo the speed tax at the cost of dedicating a CPU core to the network card via CPU pinning.</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Custom Hardware: FPGAs</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Once CPU cores are pinned and the kernel is bypassed for networking, the next bottleneck is typically the operating system itself and the CPU command execution pipeline.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Burning application logic directly with FPGAs comes next. </span></strong><span>In 2012, Optiver started experimenting with field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), which are chips that can be rewired for a specific purpose. Custom trading logic is typically written in </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/040e5e7c-49d3-408e-b8db-34a51355c443?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Hardware description language</span></a><span> and then compiled into a chip-specific logical gate configuration that can be burned onto a chip. A nice property of FPGA chips is that they can easily be rewired as needed, which is very useful for iterating on the logic.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The logic is directly encoded in physical electronic gates, so FPGAs can do in a handful of clock cycles what takes a generic CPU tens or hundreds of cycles. Processing can also be massively parallelized by data flowing through separate physical gates. This makes FPGAs significantly faster than generic CPUs, despite running at clock speeds an order of magnitude slower (typically 100s of MHz vs 3-6 GHz for modern CPUs).</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);"><span>What is bit memoization & why does it matter?</span></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The logic implemented in an FPGA is a different implementation of essentially the same algorithm from the original C++ application. Many of these algorithms can be represented with a simple request/response table, so responses don’t require anything more than a lookup.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For each expected market pattern, engineers at Optiver precompute responses in advance. When a particular market pattern is received, the chip matches the pattern and emits the prepared bits. Here’s how:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Enumerate patterns</span></strong><span>: list inbound market patterns that might arise</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Precompute:</span></strong><span> prepare a response in advance for each potential market event, typically during the FPGA design phase</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Hold behind the gate:</span></strong><span> precomputed responses are held behind a fast gate</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Drop the gate</span></strong><span>: receive an event for which there’s a precomputed response, and release the prepared bits to the exchange</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This precomputation approach allows Optiver to reduce response times into nanosecond territory.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Custom hardware: silicon/ASIC</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>FPGAs operate at lower clock frequencies than custom chips, so a logical step towards lower latencies is to build custom silicon (</span><strong><span>ASIC</span></strong><span>: Application-Specific Integrated Circuit) where clock speeds operate in the GHz territory.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Optiver began exploring custom silicon design in 2019.</span></strong><span> Building and testing ASICs takes significantly longer than building FPGAs, and involves talking to manufacturers, adapting the design to work with a manufacturer’s process, verifying prototypes, etc.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This process takes months and once the chip is done, it can’t be modified without restarting the process. On the other hand, FPGA chips are similar to the compiling of code in terms of flexiblity: the configuration is simply uploaded into a chip which is ready to be used within minutes and can be reconfigured at will.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Hardware org: small teams & full-stack scope</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Teams working on hardware projects are not so different from those on software projects: they’re trading teams which understand the domain they’re building in, and own outcomes end-to-end.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Hardware teams are very small, typically 5-10 engineers. </span></strong><span>They include those doing FPGA and ASIC work. Given their size, they are also nimble; for example, in hardware, lead times of six months-or-more for custom manufacturing are not unusual. But within small and nimble teams working with traders, it is considerably faster.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Hardware teams own the hardware stack as well as the software they build on top of it. It’s a baseline expectation for FPGA engineers at Optiver to be comfortable working in C/C++ to write software on top.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>FPGA testing is part of CI. </span></strong><span>FPGAs are tested in the same way as software; they’re part of the CI pipeline and are run against the same automated tests as software. Hardware Description Language (</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/040e5e7c-49d3-408e-b8db-34a51355c443?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>HDL</span></a><span>) code is reviewed in the same way as regular source code is reviewed, and the same monitoring and alerting procedures apply.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>AMD hardware partnership</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>AMD is best known for providing CPUs and GPUs, and is also an FPGA and custom network interface cards (NICs) provider. Optiver is a customer and also a co-development partner of AMD.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>AMD is increasingly investing in industry-specific solutions, as per HFT</span></strong><span>. This is notable as AMD’s major competitor, Intel, does not have as many such partnerships. Kevin Sprague, Optiver’s Hardware Engineering Lead, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/69eb47a6-17b5-4874-9c67-18064de4a208?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>explains</span></a><span> the need to build custom hardware:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“We operate on numerous global exchanges, each with different protocols, throttling rules and regulatory nuances. We also support various trading products and teams, such as D1 Futures, Single Stock Options (SSO), and Index, each with unique system requirements. Every product demands its own distinct approach and design tailored for the specific strategies of the team involved.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Managing this complexity means we can’t afford to rely on off-the-shelf solutions. We need tailored hardware that supports varied trading approaches while maintaining the speed and reliability our systems demand.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Building custom hardware is vital to reduce latency</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A common theme in most hardware engineering at Optiver is full ownership of all potential sources of latency; the company cares not only about peak performance, but also about latency variances. The logical step is to focus on network and physical infrastructure.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>5. Network & physical infrastructure</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Once the core trading logic is fully optimized and living in custom chips, the next biggest source of latency and latency variance is the network:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The network over which market information and market orders travel</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>All networking components, from when the order leaves the server’s network card, until it reaches the exchange endpoint</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Physical infrastructure</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver aims to own the whole physical networking stack, all the way to the exchange.</span><strong><span> </span></strong><span>This is the same principle that led to the building of FPGAs and ASICs: the company builds bespoke network hardware and cabling inside the data center in order to fully own all network infrastructure on the way to the exchange.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Link congestion is one reason to own a complete networking stack. </span></strong><span>When Optiver wants to move data from its data center to the exchange, the internet is not how this is done because it’s too unpredictable. Data traveling via the internet can follow routes with unpredictable latencies, and be delayed by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7a1e838e-f25d-46e9-b937-45002374291d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>networking congestion</span></a><span>, aka link congestion.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Dedicated fiber & wavelength leasing</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In order to circumvent network congestion, Optiver rolls out its own dedicated fiber, or rents dedicated slices of existing fiber. Multiple beams of light can travel through the same optical fiber without interference if they are at different wavelengths.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Optiver leases “wavelength” services. </span></strong><span>This means they get exclusive rights to a range of light wavelengths on a given cable, providing guaranteed bandwidth and latency.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Challenges of optical cable</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Even so, optical cables aren’t perfect; they can get cut off – and regularly do. The most common cause is construction work on land, but there are some notable cases of cables being cut by ship anchors and shark bites. Most damaged cables can be repaired in a day or two, but undersea repairs can take months.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Therefore, Optiver must ensure its redundant cable connections are as independent as possible. This means making sure they enter a landmass at different places, follow different routes, and, ideally, enter the data center building from different sides.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Optiver manages a network with around 75,000 km (46,000 miles) of fiber.</span></strong><span> These cables run along highways, powerlines, and even along the ocean floor. Management of this infrastructure is done from the Amsterdam office.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Radio</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Optiver also runs its own microwave radio network</span></strong><span>. Some parts of this network are rented from third parties. This might be surprising, until we learn a fun fact about radio vs optical latency: radio waves travel through air 30-40% faster than light travels through an optical cable. </span><em><span>This is because radio waves are a form of light traveling through air, as are optical signals traveling through glass: but glass slows the propagation of light. Radio through air travels roughly at 300,000 km/sec, and light through glass roughly at 200,000 km/sec.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On the other hand, microwaves are disrupted by snow and heavy rain, so they have to maintain a fiber connection for failover.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Shortwave radio is used to reduce latency across longer distances. </span></strong><span>Microwaves don’t travel far, so to cover longer distances, Optiver uses shortwave radio. This approach can shave off a few milliseconds of latency (compared to optical cables) over large distances. Similarly to microwaves, this comes with reliability and bandwidth caveats as radio waves can only carry limited bandwidth, so the optical cable network is still critical for bandwidth and failover reasons.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Data centers & co-locations</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The next step in reducing latency via infrastructure decisions is to place hardware as close as possible to the exchanges that Optiver is connected to. In nanosecond territory, cable lengths matter: in an optical cable, light travels about 20cm per nanosecond, so even a cable that’s a bit longer than necessary introduces latency.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Optiver runs 30-40 co-locations with various exchanges, </span></strong><span>and has servers as close as possible to electronic exchanges. Here’s a typical setup at an electronically traded exchange:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em><span>A typical exchange setup. Source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/24f7c679-d243-44c0-83f8-05882593304d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>Optiver</span></a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The exchange sends market data to all exchange participants using </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d2b78338-ff70-4ffd-8e6b-1475a5708bba?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>UDP multicast</span></a><span>, guaranteeing all members receive the information simultaneously. Traders like Optiver make their orders using TCP connections to the exchange.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>While each data center and co-location is technically self-contained and can run independently, many trading strategies require signals that aren’t locally available. For example, a trading strategy focused on ETFs in New York might need information about </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/40d466a6-dddc-43bd-bba0-cf9ecdda65cd?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>futures</span></a><span> traded in Chicago. Since that information is also latency-sensitive, you need a low-latency, guaranteed-performance connection to the data source in Chicago.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Part of why Optiver’s Platform team is such a large portion of the whole team is because they have teams managing all the details mentioned above. It is a huge undertaking to maintain almost a dozen proprietary data centers and 30-40 co-locations, while building customer hardware and cabling, planning and maintaining connections between these locations across multiple redundant links (fiber, radio).</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The business can manage this complexity with a fairly small team of a couple of hundred engineers by employing a high degree of specialization: they don’t need general purpose data centers and connections, and instead optimize for guaranteed throughput and low latency for their specific use cases.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is also exactly the type of skillset which AI labs value. Squeezing as much performance as possible from existing hardware, or rolling your own hardware to get even more performance has a similar impact on training and serving AI models as on high-frequency trading. This capability is considered an important source of competitive advantage, so the competition for talent is heated.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Models and AI now matter even more than latency</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Most market-making strategies are latency-sensitive because they are all fundamentally an </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c674f81e-a8a2-49fe-8407-8aa41fc4675e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>arbitrage opportunity</span></a><span>, or suffer from being exploited by arbitrage traders if they don’t move their prices fast enough. That’s why Optiver has had to historically obsess over latency; if not, they would fall behind competitors.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>These days, latency is the </span></strong><em><strong><span>floor,</span></strong></em><strong><span> and the differentiator is models, including AI ones. </span></strong><span>Back in the early days, having lower latency than the competition allowed for arbitrage opportunities to make risk-free profit. But as most serious players now have low-latency market access, this advantage has gone. Today, low latency is a baseline, and it takes more to make consistently profitable trades.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As such, information models are becoming the differentiator. Alex Itkin says Optiver thinks of information models in two ways:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Slow model with a fast trigger: </span></strong><span>a more complex model – often AI – runs on a slower cadence, digesting rich data. This model identifies likely scenarios, which are then memorized. When a scenario happens, the model sends a signal to the system, </span><em><span>fast</span></em><span>, and a trade is made which should be profitable.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Fast model near the edge of the network. </span></strong><span>A simpler but fast model – which could also be an AI model – runs close to the decision point, e.g. very close to an exchange. It monitors signals in realtime, and acts immediately and with low latency when it identifies a profitable scenario. This model is often a </span><em><span>distilled</span></em><span> version of a more complex model, built to run fast inference on the edge.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Today, more work goes into model work than reducing latency. </span></strong><span>There is easily 20x more engineering work happening with models and data than in efforts to further reduce latency. After all, there are only so many ways to reduce latency – the speed of light limitation applies! – but there are far more ways to gain an advantage with slow models firing triggers, or fast models running close to the edge.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>6. Engineering practices</span></h2><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Risk versus speed</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In our research, we found two factors which strongly influence engineering culture at a company like Optiver:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Approach to risk and ownership</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Move-fast mindset</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Trading carries inherent risks, especially at Optiver’s scale; even a single mistake can bankrupt a business, as shown by the</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f1acf5f4-8042-4504-8127-e843823135ed?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span> Knight Capital incident</span></a><span>. That event was a turning point for the industry, which then started to significantly increase investment in risk management tooling.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“No risk without reward” is a mantra. </span></strong><span>This came up when we talked with engineering leaders for our research, and it has two important corollaries:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Risk awareness: do not take risks blindly; make them explicitly visible</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Payoff: there must be adequate reward for taking a risk</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Below is an excerpt from an onboarding talk at Optiver which illustrates this approach.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure Optiver</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As mentioned, software at Optiver exists for the purpose of making profitable trades, and teams are encouraged to maximize the value of their trades by taking whatever approach seems most promising.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Rapid experimentation is a day-to-day practice company-wide.</span></strong><span> Teams deploy hundreds of changes to production daily. Therefore, everyone is expected to own outcomes end-to-end,</span><strong><span> </span></strong><span>and work independently across different roles and areas, as needed. So, how does Optiver reconcile this extreme ownership and rapid experimentation culture with the high-stakes environment it operates in? The business frames it as a knowledge question: </span><strong><span>if a team has all the relevant information, it’s assumed they will make the right call.</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This philosophy of trusting teams which have the right context can be tied to the risk-management approach: they make risks visible via knowledge sharing, testing, and monitoring setup.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Knowledge-sharing culture</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Ensuring individuals and teams have the right information starts with onboarding.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Optiver hires many graduates, </span></strong><span>who go through an extensive onboarding program called Optiver Global Academy where, in addition to tech onboarding, they are also taught about trading and financial fundamentals. Those graduates are soon expected to start solving real trading problems in production. New joiners are expected to start pushing changes to production within days, and to help onboard new joiners within a year.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“Quant dev” is a popular role at the company. </span></strong><span>Engineers get a very specific combination of skills that are uncommon at other tech companies. They’re performance-obsessed engineers with a solid background in trading and financial modeling.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Design reviews and architecture decisions</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Knowledge sharing continues after onboarding is over, via weekly internal tech talks, and this is a vital part of the software development lifecycle. A notable example of this are design reviews. They help teams refine designs before they start building, and an extensive testing suite provides actionable feedback while building apps. Meanwhile, robust monitoring allows the team to detect when an app misbehaves, and to take production lessons forward to the next iteration of a design.</span></p><div 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em><span>Typical development process at Optiver</span></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Significant changes start with a design review; a meeting at which a team presents their proposed changes to senior leaders whose job is to ensure the team did their homework: did they take into consideration all the relevant options and aspects of the problem?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>The teams still fully own the architectural decision making;</span></strong><span> this process is less about control and more about sharing knowledge and making informed trade-offs. Design reviews are time-consuming, so are not triggered for every change. Only those with the most impact on the architecture are reviewed.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Testing culture: pyramidal and “pre-AI”</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The expectation for everyone to push changes fast and the reality of a fairly fresh workforce means the potential exists for mistakes with disastrous financial consequences. That’s where a rock-solid testing infrastructure comes in.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Bugs are risks with no associated reward. </span></strong><span>Optiver’s automated test suite covers the whole range of the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e5bdb23b-1368-4513-8f8c-97d0a63cf8da?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>testing pyramid</span></a><span>: unit tests, automated application-level tests, end-to-end regression tests. These are built to catch functional bugs and performance regressions with backtesting and simulation tooling.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Investment was made in this before AI, and has been paying big dividends during the age of AI. Non-engineering team members such as traders and researchers regularly push code to production without having to hand over work to engineers, confident that things will work in production.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Monitoring & incident detection</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>In contrast to risk management and testing, monitoring wasn’t always top-of-mind at Optiver.</span></strong><span> Teams historically prioritized shipping changes to production over adding relevant monitoring and alerting to the system. The team was much smaller and the overall system simpler, so keeping tabs on overall performance was easier.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But as the team and overall scope has grown, it started becoming increasingly tricky to sustain nanosecond-level latencies across production with hundreds of engineers pushing production changes daily. That’s why the company has invested heavily in monitoring over the past decade.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The performance ranges that apps operate in production are incredibly tight. Their monitoring is sensitive enough to detect a change in latencies introduced by a longer-than-necessary cable. This was a real production incident!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At such latency levels, it’s sometimes hard to distinguish signal from noise. Some changes have a performance impact that’s close to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e2f28684-09c5-4860-8ee4-23394539f6d8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>stochastic noise</span></a><span>, so it can take a couple of days of monitoring to tell if a result is statistically significant.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Since they’re able to attach direct profit/loss impact to each incident, most incident prioritization decisions are based on monetary impact. While many small, inconsequential incidents get logged, incidents with a meaningful impact are very rare – maybe a few a year – and their impact is very limited. This is a remarkable level of performance, given that the company makes tens of millions of trades a day and the trading income exceeds $4.5 billion.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver gives teams full ownership and aligns their incentives, so they move at speed, with risk controls, testing, and monitoring tooling. With AI, the system comes under additional pressure, as more changes are flowing than ever at increasing speeds.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Risk management</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Risk is a key platform functionality at Optiver, and trading applications and services are enveloped by the risk management system, which monitors all apps’ signals and outputs (trade orders), and checks for unexpected behaviors. When an app is deemed to misbehave, risk management can decide to kill it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For use cases that are less latency sensitive, active trader oversight can also be involved: traders can stop apps, and tweak their system parameters based on observed performance. For latency-sensitive use cases, trading activity is automatically monitored post-trade to avoid adding latency on the hot path, and trading apps deemed to be misbehaving can be stopped.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Making risks visible and ensuring teams know how to react</span></strong><span> is woven in from building to running trading software:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Engineering culture:</span></strong><span> Systems are designed with risk in mind from day one, via knowledge sharing and design review sessions.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Robust testing and monitoring infrastructure: </span></strong><span>ensures risks are identified as soon as possible during the software development process</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Central risk platform: </span></strong><span>In a decentralized, federated team model, a central risk platform ensures a team has the “big picture” of the system’s behavior, and can react when needed.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These multiple layers of protection are Optiver’s version of a well-understood </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cdf77efe-78ed-4945-b9d1-b93019eaa93b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Swiss Cheese model</span></a><span>, with each layer focusing on one cause of problems, and all the layers together covering the full problem surface area.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>7. AI at Optiver</span></h2><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Inflection point</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The engineering team at Optiver has used AI-assisted coding heavily – and Cursor in particular – since the early days of the technology. After the arrival of Claude Code with Opus 4.5 in late 2025, and stronger agentic capabilities, adoption took off at the prop shop.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At that point, it was no longer a case of engineers playing around with cutting-edge tooling. David Gross, tech lead on the Options trading team, was inspired to look into agentic coding more deeply by a London trader who spun up multiple agents concurrently to automate work.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Future of agentic coding</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver’s tech leadership doesn’t see AI coding as only a way of being more efficient. It’s also about rethinking how software is built, which changes how teams work together on building and shipping software. For example, David conceives an autonomous agentic coding loop in terms of an optimization problem with three axes:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Intent</span></strong><span>: defines the optimization objective, including documentation and architectural principles feeding into the prompt</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Back pressure:</span></strong><span> constrains the solution space via tests, code reviews, and making sure a solution is correct</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Velocity: </span></strong><span>limits how quickly an agent can iterate. More generally, how long does it take to find out if a generated solution works?</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Any improvement to one of the axes represents a compounding investment because future AI-coding sessions will reuse it. Optiver’s leadership believes that convincing teams to improve the three axes is critical, as it builds the foundation of a future development platform. A big challenge here is that it’s “meta work” about redefining the work itself at a place where the primary focus is making profitable trades.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Adoption</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>At the time of publication, AI-coding adoption and investment isn’t universal at Optiver in the three axes, </span></strong><span>despite AI-coding tools being generally reasonably well adopted by teams and supported by the Platform team. This is a tension between short-term incentives and longer-term investment in a fully agentic coding platform.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Improving them requires time away from day-to-day projects, but a big part of engineers’ compensation is tied to trading profits (day-to-day projects), meaning teams are invested in a very literal sense, so must choose wisely between slowing down and investing in AI workflows, or maintaining business-as-usual and protecting their comp.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Meanwhile, senior management sees a fully agentic coding ecosystem as an unmissable opportunity: if they don’t take it, the company will pay the price commercially when competitors do.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Optiver’s culture of owning trading problems end-to-end necessarily limits AI adoption – and perhaps that’s a good thing. </span></strong><span>It’s refreshing to see a company not madly rushing to adopt a new technology just because everyone else is. If Optiver’s leadership believes that faster AI adoption is critical, it’ll be necessary to resolve the friction of engineers focusing on business outcomes, and being highly pragmatic about adopting AI tools that improve them.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>AI tooling stack</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To support teams improving their solutions along the three axes, the platform team has standardized key components:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Model gateway</span></strong><span>, giving everyone centralized access and cost control.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Agent + MCP platform</span></strong><span>. Teams quickly started building their own MCPs around services they wanted agents to utilize most. To avoid running them on their own desktops, the Platform team provides a centralized place to host MCP servers and agents. Some were common across many teams, so the platform team made them part of the platform offering.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/38e2fed3-5d8c-441e-91ed-29c5597b6052?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>LangSmith</span></a></strong><span> is included in the platform, providing teams with observability and evals of agents.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These basic building blocks, on top of which teams build their own agents, enable the platform team to keep costs under control, which is becoming important due to AI token costs.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>How does this look in practice?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver has AI agents running in production with a major caveat: </span><strong><span>AI agents are only allowed to do a small subset of operations within their production area.</span></strong><span> Why? It’s all about risk.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver’s platform teams provide guidance to teams via </span><strong><span>AI use cases,</span></strong><span> of which there’s a detailed taxonomy, and also a list of </span><strong><span>restrictions</span></strong><span> specifying what agents can and can’t do.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It seems to work. At Optiver, more non-engineers ship to production than before, but without production incidents which cause negative financial impacts. They say it’s because their longstanding focus on automated testing has proven valuable in the era of AI: every production change goes through thorough testing, where mistakes are usually caught.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>AI seems to be accelerating the “researcher-to-engineer-to-production” pipeline. </span></strong><span>In the past, it took a researcher/trader, plus an engineer working together to get strategies into production. Today, partly thanks to AI, traders and researchers ship strategy implementation to production by themselves.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>8. Hiring, career development & culture</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Engineers account for roughly 40% of the circa 2,200 workforce at Optiver. This might seem a fairly low percentage given algorithmic trading is the entirety of what they do, but there’s a fluidity between roles which means non-engineering folks also contribute to the trading system.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Europe was always Optiver’s center of gravity, but the company has been investing heavily in the US in recent years, and the tech team there has more than doubled in the last four years. Many teams are located across multiple locations to align with exchanges’ opening hours.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver has a career ladder similar to that of Big Tech, with levels from L3 to L7:</span></p><div
