style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver has a career ladder with four dimensions which apply at all levels:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Technical Prowess</span></strong><span>: expectations of technical expertise</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Business Acumen</span></strong><span>: expectations of business understanding</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Responsibility / Autonomy</span></strong><span>: expectations of independent working</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Depth / Sphere of Impact:</span></strong><span> expectations of wide-ranging work</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>The original strategy: “hire 22-year-olds”</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the early years, Optiver’s hiring strategy was to focus on new grads and growing them into specific quant-dev roles, Alex Itkin told us: “We built a multi-billion dollar company doing nothing but hiring 22-year-olds.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Core technical competencies are critical for job candidates to possess, but plenty of roles at Optiver need skills that are not taught at universities. The business has always looked to hire candidates who, given a problem, are able to work through potential options and trade-offs before getting to implementation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The best predictor of long-term career success at Optiver, according to David, is not actually core technical skill. Actually, it’s having the personal drive to solve problems and get things done, and flexibility in the face of adversity.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Today: hiring experienced engineers</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As the company and its overall scope have grown, Optiver has hired more experienced engineers. Today, the company hires experienced engineers at a similar rate to Big Tech and other trading firms.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Hiring competition</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver wasn’t unique in the industry for its policy of hiring young professionals, and the competition for talent is always fierce among prop shops. Also, these days, the industry is becoming much more high-profile and visible to job seekers, and many candidates do interviews at multiple prop trading shops during their job hunt.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Everyone is chasing the same top talent against competition from outside the financial sector, too. It used to be Big Tech companies that Optiver had an edge over, with its less bureaucratic, more cash-rich compensation structure. But these days, the strongest rivals for talent are AI labs.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Onboarding feedback loop</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>New hires enter a structured program called the ‘Global Optiver Academy,’ covering the fundamentals of business and finance, in addition to standard technical onboarding. After formal training, new hires join their team and get mentors who help them push their first changes to production within a few weeks.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The onboarding process itself is pretty standard in tech, but what’s interesting is that Optiver built a feedback loop between onboarding and hiring, with analytics teams analyzing onboarding cohorts. This is used to tweak hiring guidelines and interviewer training.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>9. Takeaways</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Here are the main takeaways we’ve taken after talking with the Optiver team, split as observations from the three of us working with the Optiver team (Ivan, Jesse and Gergely:)</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>The impact of optimizing for low latency</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>From Ivan Klaric:</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As an engineer, it’s interesting that latency optimization leads to the progression from high-performance C++ apps to custom chips. I love the “method in the madness” vibe.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Narrative-wise, a major detail is that everyone at Optiver is a trader, doing whatever necessary to make profitable trades. This drives the low-ceremony, extreme ownership culture, which in turn creates interesting tech stories like Linux kernel tweaks, custom networking equipment, FPGAs, ASICs, etc; basically, whatever it takes to make the best trade quicker than competitors.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The incentives are interesting. The nature of the business strongly incentivizes the heavy investment in testing, monitoring, and risk tooling. The business offers big bonuses which in turn drive extreme ownership culture, which can be both a curse and a blessing: it makes the leap into an AI-native world with collapsed roles a more natural progression, but the incentives can cause people to push back against the change.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>A different software engineering role inside of Optiver</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>Jesse Spevack shares:</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>AI means engineers are not the only ones writing code at Optiver today. Traders, researchers, and software engineers used to have stricter boundaries between roles, but Optiver’s researchers and traders have math and science backgrounds, while Cursor and Claude Code make producing code cheap. So, they can pair their domain knowledge and skills with AI.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That doesn’t mean Optiver no longer needs software engineers. More of the team can produce code and trading strategies, but one mistake could still bankrupt the company. The tricky part is verification; perhaps Optiver’s platform engineers, on top of managing the company’s extreme latency and performance demands, will have even more work to do on validation, safety and risk systems. This work on validation, safety and risk systems keeps Optiver at the forefront of the prop trading industry.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver controls its whole stack, from the integrated circuit layer up through network fiber and on-prem servers, to a global platform that enables all its market activity. The trading strategies come from researchers and traders with deep math and machine learning expertise, with a decade of “hill-climbing” on latency, from kernel bypass to custom ASICs. All of this is a moat that would surely take a tremendous amount of capital to compete with.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Similarities and differences vs “regular” tech companies and startups</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>Finally, from me (Gergely):</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One of the biggest differences Optiver has compared to most tech companies is how it has no external customers. This creates very different dynamics: there are no deadlines from things that external customers would expect, but at the same time, there’s ongoing feedback about how much profit each trade and software feature made.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With such a different set of constraints, it was interesting for me to look at what is similar in engineering approaches, compared to tech companies with external customers (like B2C or B2B tech companies):</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Design reviews are important. </span></strong><span>Bugs and mistakes cost money, so Optiver does reviews early on in the planning process to make sure they build the right thing, and get input to catch possible issues. This is similar to how today even leading AI companies like Anthropic do product review documents (PRDs) for complex, high-impact projects, as we covered </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/037b4f87-2e5c-4621-bf5c-63df80c8be3c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>in our Anthropic deepdive.</span></a></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>CI/CD remains in-place. </span></strong><span>Verifying that software runs correctly is done with continuous integration and continuous deployment, and all the tests that run through these</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Small teams across the business. </span></strong><span>Teams are small across the org, at 5-10 engineers, even inside areas like hardware engineering.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And some of the major differences to how SaaS tech businesses, and many startups operate:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Full control of hardware </span></strong><em><strong><span>and</span></strong></em><strong><span> software. </span></strong><span>Engineers at Optiver work on optimizations at the kernel level, and produce custom hardware to further reduce latency across their system. It’s rare for tech companies to get into producing custom hardware for their own, internal usage!</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Formal training after onboarding. </span></strong><span>Most tech companies and startups throw new hires into the deep water. Optiver, meanwhile, has a “Global Optiver Academy” teaching the fundamentals of business and finance to new joiners. I assume this is because many new engineer hires will not be up to speed with these topics: but they’ll need it to succeed at the company!</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Dealing with risk is part of decision making, across the company. </span></strong><span>Optiver – and other trading firms – are far more aware of the financial damage software bugs can cause, thanks to the cautionary tale of Knight Capital being destroyed with a single bad deploy. So while the lack of external customers would theoretically allow Optiver to move as fast as they please, wanting to minimize the risk of deployments means that they put in guardrails and checks to avoid software issues causing expensive incidents.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>I hope you enjoyed this deepdive into a niche, but exciting industry. Thanks very much to Alex Itkin, Pat Cooney, David Gross and the Optiver team for their time and input!</span></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;margin-bottom: 16px;overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>This post is only for paying subscribers of </em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzbGV0dGVyLnByYWdtYXRpY2VuZ2luZWVyLmNvbT91dG1fY2FtcGFpZ249ZW1haWwtaG9tZSZyPTM2eGwxbyIsInAiOjIwOTkzNDkzMiwicyI6NDU4NzA5LCJmIjpmYWxzZSwidSI6MTkzMDQzMTQ4LCJpYXQiOjE3ODY0NjU1MzMsImV4cCI6MjEwMjA0MTUzMywiaXNzIjoicHViLTAiLCJzdWIiOiJsaW5rLXJlZGlyZWN0In0.-N6-z35S8-BySv0x_oIesR6cOMpk59gzssEeaMDdHz8?" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Pragmatic Engineer</a><em>. More than half of the traffic online now comes from software that acts on a person’s behalf, requests a page, and leaves without engaging with any ads or subscriptions [2].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Cloudflare seeks to change this.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As you might be aware, Cloudflare sits between a large share of the world’s websites and everything requesting them. It works as a reverse proxy that each request passes through before it reaches the origin server [1]. This lets Cloudflare read a request and act on it early. Over the past year, the company has used this position to sort automated traffic by what it does, to verify the identity behind a request, and, most recently, to collect payment for a request through an open protocol named x402 [1].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we will go through Cloudflare’s solution in the following five steps:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The web’s usual way of earning value leans on human attention, and agent traffic changes it fundamentally.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A look at Cloudflare’s initial solution around blocking automated traffic and then charging for each crawl.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Settling identity, permission, and payment inside a single request.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A look at how x402 exchange completes this settlement.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The x402 exchange completes this settlement through a short back-and-forth over ordinary HTTP</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The costs and open questions of this approach</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" justify"><em><span>Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from Cloudflare. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>The Attention Model</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For most of its history, websites made money after a request rather than during it. A browser asked for a page, and the server returned it at no charge. The value arrived later, once a person saw an advertisement, bought a subscription, or came back for another visit [1]. The request itself stayed free, and this setup funded a large part of the Internet.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A growth in agent traffic is changing this dramatically. An agent is software that acts on a person’s behalf, which in practice means it requests a page or a data feed once, takes what it needs, and finishes in a single pass. It moves past advertisements, operates outside any subscription, and completes its task before a site has a chance to earn from that attention [1]. Each of the three old settlement points depended on a person staying long enough to be counted, so software traffic leaves those points idle.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The strain here is that this kind of traffic is now fast becoming the majority. More than half of the requests reaching websites come from software rather than people [2]. This means that request volume climbs while revenue stays flat.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To make things clear, parts of the Internet were already charging by usage before any of this. Cloud services and APIs have been sold by the call and by the hour for years, though only to a buyer the seller already knew, who signed up and received an API key [1]. Charging an anonymous caller a fraction of a cent for a single request stayed impractical, because collecting such a small payment once cost more than the payment returned [1].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If the value used to settle downstream of the request, the natural question is which party is positioned to move that settlement back onto the request. The answer starts with where Cloudflare sits.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>The Proxy Layer</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A reverse proxy is a server that stands in front of other servers and receives requests on their behalf. Since Cloudflare operates as a reverse proxy for a large portion of the web, a request headed for one of those sites reaches Cloudflare’s network first and passes through it on the way to the origin [1]. The origin is the site’s own server, the machine that ultimately holds the page or runs the API.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On a side note, the position of a proxy is more general-purpose than caching. Caching stores a copy of a response so it can be served quickly the next time, and it is just one of the many useful things a proxy can do. From the same middle position, a request can also be read, classified, checked, and acted on before it continues to the origin. This broader capability is quite consequential at Cloudflare’s scale. [2].</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" a request early depends on first knowing what the request is for. This is a classification problem. Let us see how Cloudflare handles this.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Traffic Classification</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Before any rule can apply to an agent, the traffic has to be sorted by what it does. Cloudflare’s taxonomy groups automated traffic by behavior rather than by the single label “AI”. Three behaviors impact the key policy decisions [4].</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Search covers behavior that builds an index of a site so an engine can answer questions about it later. This behavior is responsible for sending referral visitors back.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>An agent covers behavior that acts in real time on a person’s behalf, usually with a human waiting for the result. Think of it like an assistant fetching a page during a conversation.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Training covers behavior that takes content to train or fine-tune a model, where the content is absorbed into the model rather than pointing a visitor back.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These three appear identical in a raw request log, yet they carry very different consequences for a site’s business.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A single crawler can also perform more than one of these behaviors, but this separation lets them record all of them[4]. A crawler that both builds a search index and gathers training data is tracked as doing both, which lets a site owner reason about the full set of things that the crawler does on their pages.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Cloudflare classifies further behaviors as well, including checkout actions and data collection, and it also lets a site express what a bot may store and reshare after accessing a page [4].</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: the proxy position and a way to classify what arrives, let us now look at Cloudflare’s first attempts at implementing a policy.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Blocking and Charging</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Cloudflare’s first solution was a simple one. A single control lets a site block automated AI traffic outright. This protected the content and left the earning model untouched. Blocking answers the question of access, yet it does not rebuild the revenue that the old bargain provided.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The second solution added a middle path.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Pay Per Crawl lets a website allow a crawler, block it, or charge it a flat per-request price, with Cloudflare handling the billing as the merchant of record [5]. A site owner could keep a crawler out, let it through, or attach a price to its access, all from one setting. This turned the binary of block-or-allow into three options and gave content owners a way to earn from crawler access at network scale [5].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A year on, Cloudflare made an adjustment to its own model. The company argued that a crawl is a weak measure of value, because a single page might be crawled once and then cited in thousands of AI answers, or crawled repeatedly and cited in none [3]. It backed the argument with a figure from its own network, that more than half of the crawl traffic from well-behaved bots goes to re-fetching pages that have stayed the same since the last visit [3]. Counting crawls, then, counts something that only loosely tracks the value delivered.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So the unit of payment began to move from the crawl toward the use, an approach Cloudflare describes as Pay Per Use. It is candidly framed as an experiment at this point [3]. This is because while pricing the outcome aligns payment with value more closely than pricing the fetch, it is also harder to measure.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>The Request Layer</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The design goal for recent changes is to resolve identity, permission, and payment inside a single request, at the edge, before the origin responds.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Three main concerns are considered over here:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Identity:</span></strong><span> The traditional identifier, the User-Agent string, can be set to any value by the caller, so it offers weak assurance. Cloudflare’s answer is Web Bot Auth, an authentication method that uses cryptographic signatures in HTTP messages to verify that a request comes from a particular automated source [7]. In practice, the operator signs its request with a private key and publishes the matching public key at a known location, and Cloudflare validates the signature at the edge [8]. A valid signature stands in for a reliable identity, which replaces a guess with a verifiable claim.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Permission:</span></strong><span> This is expressed through the behavior classification already covered and through the preferences a site sets about how its content may be used [4].</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Payment:</span></strong><span> This comes last and is attached to the request through x402. We will cover this in detail in the next section.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>All three concerns resolve at the edge, so the origin receives a request only once identity, permission, and payment have been settled [1]. The metering and settlement are taken away from the website’s own servers. What stays with the site owner is the part that matters to them, which is their rules, their prices, and their revenue [1].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To summarize:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Identity answers who is making the request, through a signed and verified claim.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Permission answers whether this behavior is allowed on these pages, through the classification and content preferences.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Payment answers whether the caller has paid the stated price through the x402 exchange.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These pieces sit at different stages of maturity. Identity verification through Web Bot Auth is available today at the edge [7], while the Monetization Gateway that brings the payment piece together is open as a waitlist rather than a shipped product [1].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The key takeaway is that when one component sits in the middle of a flow, the concerns that are common across every request are collected at that point. Authentication, authorization, and billing consolidating at a gateway is the same pattern that appears in service meshes and middleware.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>The x402 Exchange</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The x402 protocol makes it possible to pay over HTTP. It takes its name from a status code that has been part of the HTTP standard for a long time [1]. The code is 402, and it means Payment Required. Sites behind Cloudflare already send more than a billion of these responses on an average day, which shows how often a machine requests something priced and receives a message that a payment is due [6].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below that shows the overall setup:</span></p><div through a short sequence that can be compared to a small state machine [1].</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A client requests a resource that sits behind a price.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Rather than returning the resource, the server responds with 402 and a small payload stating the price, the accepted asset, and where to pay.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The client re-sends the same request with proof of payment attached.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A facilitator verifies the payment, and the server returns the resource.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Two properties make this suitable for machine traffic. The payment amounts can be very small because the protocol adds almost no overhead to the request. And the payment itself serves as the credential, so a buyer with no prior relationship can access the content by showing the proof of payment [1]. This property is the one that matches an anonymous agent passing through once, since it removes the signup step that per-seat licensing and API keys always required.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The negotiation process is handled inside ordinary requests and responses, with a redirect to a checkout page absent and a separate payment API absent [1]. Nothing was added at the protocol level, since the 402 code has been part of HTTP for decades. What changed is that a settlement angle now exists that makes collecting a fraction of a cent practical.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Costs and Limits</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Resolving identity, permission, and payment at the edge means one proxy performs those functions for a large share of the web at once [1]. Cloudflare presents that responsibility as an advantage for settling everything inside one request. But it can also be seen as a potential risk when so much runs through a single provider.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Cloudflare also states several limits plainly:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Trust that travels with a request may reach only the traffic that can afford to be identifiable, and small or privacy-sensitive sources of traffic need other building blocks, such as private rate limiting [4].</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Usage-based payment helps a site that already has demand, and does little for a small site whose real difficulty is discoverability rather than monetization, which leaves that site weighing visibility against giving content away [4].</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Collecting a payment through this exchange depends on callers built to recognize and honor the 402 response. Therefore, the revenue depends on adoption within the ecosystem. [6].</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Pricing an outcome rather than a crawl aligns payment with value, but it is also harder to measure and verify. This is the reason Cloudflare frames the shift to Pay-Per-Use as an experiment [3].</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Lastly, Cloudflare argues that crawlers combining several purposes under one identity reduce transparency for a site. This is because the site cannot tell why it is being accessed [4]. While the argument is sound based on technical merits, it also aligns with Cloudflare’s commercial interest in separated, verifiable traffic.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>None of these costs undoes the shift. They simply mark the current trade-offs that website owners should consider before adopting it.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The web is moving value settlement from after the request to inside it. For most of the web’s history, a request was served free, and value was settled later through human attention. However, agent traffic, which now comprises the majority of requests, leaves that later settlement with nowhere to land [2].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Cloudflare’s response is to resolve four things from its position as a reverse proxy: seeing what a request is through classification, verifying who sent it through Web Bot Auth, enforcing the site’s rules, and settling payment through the x402 exchange, all before the origin responds [1][4][7].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Identity verification lives at the edge today, and the payment gateway opens as a waitlist [1][7]. The open questions around concentration, reach, adoption, and how to price an outcome are worth tracking as the model develops.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: item.title: Relentless Forward Progress
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Relentless Forward Progress

Mike Fisher

“The hardest stretches of running a team are not sprints. They are ultras: the long downturn, the slow turnaround, the market that stays bad for six quarters straight. None is solved by a single heroic burst. They are survived, or not, by how you manage the long middle, when the adrenaline is gone and the only skill left is suffering productively while metering what you have.”_ _

#Leadership Management Wellbeing
item.description: Relentless Forward Progress

item.title: The Antithesis Principle
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Antithesis Principle

Shreyas Doshi

(1) If you want to help people learn something, look into making it engaging / entertaining. This first one is the easier, more obvious conclusion. (2) It is actually not in your best interest to be the kind of person who can only learn from entertaining content. Nor to be the kind of person that needs any sort of entertainment as a prerequisite for learning. The vast majority of smart people will never consider this second conclusion.

#CareerGrowth
item.description: The Antithesis Principle

item.title: Middle Management Roles Are Also A Trap
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Middle Management Roles Are Also A Trap

Will Larson

“If you’re willing to embrace this fact that a little bit of time in middle management roles is important preparation to become an executive, but spending a great deal of time in middle management only prepares you for further middle management roles–and makes you less effective as a potential executive–then the AI-driven shift in managerial fads might be a threat to your current role, but it’s likely to improve your chances to succeed as an executive.”

#Management CareerGrowth
item.description: Middle Management Roles Are Also A Trap

item.title: A Practical Guide To Rapid Onboarding
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
A Practical Guide To Rapid Onboarding

Steve Huynh

“After nearly two decades at Amazon, operating as a Principal Engineer, often parachuting into complex, high stakes projects, I’ve developed a system to cut through this chaos. In this article, I’ll share with you that exact framework to help you get up to speed unbelievably fast.”

#Management Guide Onboarding
item.description: A Practical Guide To Rapid Onboarding

item.title: Growing As An Engineer In A World Of AI
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Growing As An Engineer In A World Of AI

Norberto Lopes

“There’s a lot of buzz that AI means companies only want seniors now. That there’s no room left for early career engineers. I don’t think that’s true. The thing actually worth worrying about isn’t whether you’ll get hired, it’s whether you keep learning in a world of AI, now that it removes the friction where that learning used to happen. And that, thankfully, is a choice you get to make.”

#AI CareerGrowth
item.description: Growing As An Engineer In A World Of AI

item.title: Agentic Code Quality
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Agentic Code Quality

Addy Osmani

“For much of human history, we’ve evaluated code quality via code review: someone reads what you wrote and makes sure it’s clean, thoughtful, fast, understandable, and tests well. For agents, that approach doesn’t scale well; there’s just too much code for anyone to read. As a result, more and more of our quality checks have to happen in the harness, environment, and operating system around the agent. Software quality now depends on the constraints you set around your agents.”

#AI CodeQuality Agents
item.description: Agentic Code Quality

item.title: Beyond Happy Path Engineering: Databases
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Beyond Happy Path Engineering: Databases

Gabor Koos

“This series is about making your programs more resilient. Each post looks at one part of the system we take for granted: networks, time, databases, storage, users, dependencies, deployments, queues, and concurrency. The question is always the same: what assumptions are we making here, and what should we do when they stop being true?”

#Databases DeepDive
item.description: Beyond Happy Path Engineering: Databases

However, the problem is much deeper. It often sits inside the component that decides which posts become part of a user’s feed in the first place.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Consider the scale of the decision. When you open a feed, the platform has a few hundred milliseconds to select a handful of posts from hundreds of millions of candidates. Scoring every candidate with an expensive model burns through the time budget. To get over this, the social media platforms rely on engagement, which is a cheap and somewhat reliable proxy for judging relevance. Such a proxy is easy to measure and optimize against, and it powered a generation of recommendation systems.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" problem is that this type of engagement is also easy to manufacture. For example, a post that opens with “comment DONE if you’re a real engineer” collects clicks and replies while delivering little value. But a ranking function tuned to reward interaction will promote it even though it is clearly an engagement bait. For years, the countermeasures against this were heuristics and demotions applied after ranking, but such an approach hasn’t eliminated the problem. Accounts producing bait always find ways around such measures.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Over the past two years, LinkedIn, Meta, and YouTube, three of the largest platforms, have tried to address the root of the problem. All of them have attempted to rebuild the retrieval stage around the meaning of content, matching posts to people by what a post is about and how it relates to a reader’s interests. The idea is that once the relevance depends on semantic meaning, the tactics built for engagement farming lose their potency. However, the three companies have taken three different directions to solve the same problem, which provides us with an opportunity to understand things from multiple perspectives.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we will work through the following points:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Why feeds relied on engagement signals for so long, and where that approach reached its limits.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How embeddings match users and content by meaning.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>LinkedIn’s consolidation of five retrieval systems into a single language-model retriever.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Meta’s opposite choice of keeping a large family of specialized models arranged as a funnel.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>YouTube’s generative approach, where the system produces the identifier of the next item.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The cold-start problem, and why pretraining helps most when a user’s history is thin.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The tradeoffs each design carries, and the limits of the engagement-bait result.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><em><span>Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Engagement Signals</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Every large feed runs on a two-step pipeline:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Retrieval: </span></strong><span>This step reduces hundreds of millions of candidates down to roughly a thousand. It has to be cheap because it touches the entire corpus.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Ranking: </span></strong><span>This step spends real compute ordering those survivors into the sequence you scroll.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Most of the recent architectural changes sit in retrieval, so that is where we will focus more.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For years, retrieval relied on behavioral signals. The system recorded which posts a user clicked, watched, and reacted to, then retrieved content that resembled those interactions or resembled the behavior of similar users. This approach scales well and produces reasonable feeds.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, it also has a weakness.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When a system optimizes a single measurable objective, it tends to optimize the literal metric rather than the intent behind it. As mentioned, engagement is a proxy for relevance, and a proxy can be optimized directly. A retrieval stage tuned on interaction counts will surface whatever maximizes interaction counts, and engagement bait is the content that does exactly that. For example, content designed to trigger a click or a reply scores highly on the measured signal while contributing little to the experience the platform aims to deliver.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Suppressing such content through demotions and rules tries to treat the symptom without fixing the underlying disease. The retrieval stage still keeps bringing up the same material. A more durable fix changes what retrieval measures in the first place, and this happens by moving from behavior to meaning.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Semantic Retrieval</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The alternative is to retrieve content by its semantic content rather than by its interaction history. The ability to make this possibility depends on embeddings.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An embedding is a list of numbers that positions an item as a point in a high-dimensional space, arranged so that related items land near one another. For example, a post about fixing a leaking tap and a post about reducing water waste sit close together even when they share no keywords, because their meanings are related. In more technical terms, the embedding reflects the relationship captured during model training.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To use embeddings for retrieval, platforms apply a dual-encoder design, sometimes called a two-tower model.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>One encoder converts a user, along with their profile and recent activity, into a point in the space.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A second encoder converts each post into a point in the same space.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Since the two encoders operate independently, a platform can compute every post embedding in advance and store it in an index. At request time, it computes the user embedding and runs a nearest-neighbor search to find the closest posts, which keeps retrieval fast across an enormous corpus.</span></p><div design comes from what the embeddings encode. A keyword system matches surface tokens, so it links “electrical engineering” to other posts containing those words. An embedding produced by a language model reflects associations present in its training data, which lets it link an “electrical engineer” to other concepts like grid optimization and renewable energy infrastructure, even when the exact terms differ.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This same pattern appears well beyond social feeds. Search ranking, retrieval-augmented generation, and product recommendation all use two-tower retrieval. The model here transfers to a wide range of systems a developer might build.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>LinkedIn, Meta, and YouTube all adopt semantic retrieval, but they diverge in how they have built their respective solutions. Let us look at them in more detail.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Unified Retrieval</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>LinkedIn’s feed previously drew candidates from separate retrieval systems, each with its own index and its own optimization logic [1].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One source supplied a chronological view of network activity, another handled trending posts by geography, another ran collaborative filtering, and several more produced embedding-based candidates. The setup worked, but maintaining five parallel systems led to rising engineering costs. Also, the sources were optimized independently rather than toward a single coherent objective.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In March 2026, LinkedIn replaced those systems with a single retrieval model built on a fine-tuned version of Meta’s LLaMA-3 [1]. The model acts as a dual encoder, converting both members and posts into one shared embedding space. It serves the entire feed through nearest-neighbor search at sub-50-millisecond latency for its member base [1].</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: model processes text, while a recommendation system runs on structured features such as view counts, engagement rates, work history, and post metadata. member becomes a passage describing their profile, skills, and an ordered sequence of recently engaged posts, and a post becomes a passage describing its author, text, and engagement statistics.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We can also take a more general idea from LinkedIn’s approach. When the team fed raw popularity counts directly into the prompts, the numbers had almost no correlation with the model’s relevance scores, because large integers entered the model as arbitrary tokens. Converting each count into a ranked bucket, expressed as a percentage that the model could process in context, raised the correlation sharply and improved retrieval accuracy by roughly fifteen percent [1].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The takeaway from this is that the model is often the part that works, and the surrounding representation of the data is where the real effort goes.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As we can see, consolidation is one answer to solve the retrieval question. However, Meta made a different choice.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Ranking Funnels</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Meta arranges Instagram’s recommendation system as a multi-stage funnel, consisting of an ecosystem of more than a thousand models supporting it [3]. Candidates pass through a sequence of stages, and each stage applies a more expensive model to a smaller set of surviving candidates [2].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The funnel runs through four steps:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Retrieval gathers candidates from many sources across the platform.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Early-stage ranking uses a lightweight two-tower model to narrow that set.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Late-stage ranking applies a heavier model to the remaining finalists.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A final pass adjusts the result for diversity and integrity.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Where LinkedIn moved toward meaning by consolidating, Meta pursues it through specialization.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In Meta’s approach, the late-stage model predicts many possible user actions at once, and a value model combines those predictions into a single score [4]. That combination adds weight for positive actions, such as a likely save, and subtracts weight for predicted negative actions, such as a “See Fewer Posts Like This” tap [4].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The basic objective of this extends past raw engagement to include signals about content a user would prefer to avoid.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" one many production recommenders resemble, which makes it a useful reference point. Many competing objectives, including engagement, diversity, integrity, and creator fairness, are easier to tune and audit as separate stages than as one model. Of course, the cost to this is operational complexity, which is the exact complexity LinkedIn set out to reduce.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To summarize, both companies looked at semantic retrieval and made opposite conclusions about how much to consolidate. However, YouTube, the third platform we are looking at, questioned whether retrieval needs to search a stored index at all.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Generative Retrieval</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>YouTube took a third route that removes the search index from retrieval altogether [5].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The system, called PLUM, assigns every video a Semantic ID, a short sequence of discrete codes derived from the video’s own content [5]. Videos with similar content receive similar codes, so the identifier carries information about the item rather than acting as a random label.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>PLUM then adapts a pretrained language model (from the Gemini family) by adding these Semantic IDs to its vocabulary and continuing to train it on video metadata and user activity [5]. After this adaptation, the model performs retrieval as a generation task. Given a user’s recent history, it produces the Semantic IDs of the videos that the user is likely to watch next, decoding several candidate identifiers through beam search, and the system maps each identifier back to a real video [5].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div however, introduces a failure mode that the index-based designs avoid, which is generating an identifier that maps to no video, and PLUM reports keeping that rate below five percent after fine-tuning [5].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The payoff from this solution appears in coverage. Measured against the previous production system, PLUM surfaced a far wider range of long-tail videos, and on YouTube Shorts, it raised panel click-through by 4.96 percent [5]. The architecture also inverts where the parameters live. The prior system stored most of its parameters in large embedding tables, while PLUM holds most of its parameters in the network itself [5].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Ultimately, the three designs converge on one payoff in the cold-start problem.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Cold Start</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A recommendation system faces the cold-start problem whenever a user arrives with little or no history. Behavioral retrieval has little to work with in this situation, because it depends on past interactions to find similar content, so new users historically saw generic material until their activity accumulated enough signal.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Semantic retrieval changes this.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Since a language model carries associations from pretraining, it can infer plausible interests from a profile alone. A member who lists a role in electrical engineering can be matched to content on grid optimization and energy infrastructure before clicking anything, using associations the model acquired during training rather than signals from that member’s own activity [1].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" capability also comes with a limit.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An inference drawn from a sparse profile can be wrong, and it can compress a person into a stereotype built from whatever their profile most resembles. The strength and the weakness have the same source, which is that the model fills gaps with prior associations. LinkedIn’s reported results fit this picture. The overall lift from the new system was modest, while the gains concentrated among new and low-connection members, which is exactly the group a meaning-based system can serve when behavioral history is sparse [1].</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Design Tradeoffs</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Every one of these designs has an associated cost and tradeoffs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The first is consolidation against specialization. LinkedIn’s single model is simpler to maintain and aligns retrieval with ranking, while Meta’s many-model funnel gives independent control over each objective and provides natural redundancy. A single model also raises a more difficult rollback question, because five specialized systems offered five independent places to intervene when one of them regressed on a case such as trending content.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The second tradeoff is related to cost. Language-model embeddings capture richer associations than the lightweight methods they replaced. However, they consume more compute to produce and serve. As LinkedIn’s popularity-count finding showed, the model is rarely the bottleneck, and the load moves to the data pipeline, the feature representation, and the serving path.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The third tradeoff sits between the generative and index-based approaches. Generative retrieval composes items from compact codes and removes the large embedding table, at the cost of a failure mode where the model can produce an identifier for a video that does not exist. Index-based retrieval avoids that failure mode, but requires storage and maintenance of the index.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height:
