reduces the leverage of bait rather than removing it, since a system can still be gamed by content engineered to match high-value topics. Also, these three designs are points of emphasis on shared scaffolding more than pure types. YouTube still ranks candidates in stages, LinkedIn’s retriever feeds a separate ranking model, and Meta continues to explore generative methods.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Social media feeds are transforming retrieval approaches from behavioral engagement to semantic meaning. This helps reduce the leverage of engagement bait as a property of the architecture.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, the three largest platforms adopted the same underlying idea and built it in three ways.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>LinkedIn consolidated five retrieval systems into a single language-model dual encoder and searches one shared embedding space.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Meta kept a large family of specialized models arranged as a staged funnel with a multi-objective value model.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>YouTube generates the identifier of the next item through an adapted language model and removes the retrieval index.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The reason these choices differ comes down to data.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A text-rich professional network, a multi-objective media platform, and a video service with an enormous item corpus each favor a different design, and each team optimized for the structure of their specific data.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>References:</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>[1]</span><a item.title: Beyond happy path engineering: Time
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Beyond happy path engineering: Time

Gabor Koos

37 minutes by Gabor Koos Gabor explains why time is more complicated in production systems than it first appears. He distinguishes wall-clock, monotonic, logical, and business time, showing when each should be used. He also covers clock drift, expiration, scheduled jobs, time zones, competing updates, and reconciliation. The main lesson is to treat time as a design boundary and make its assumptions explicit.
item.description: Beyond happy path engineering: Time

item.title: How to create your own decentralized messenger protocol
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How to create your own decentralized messenger protocol

Michał Karbowiak

15 minutes by Michał Karbowiak Michał guides on building a simple decentralized messaging protocol using federation. He covers server discovery, user identities, end-to-end encryption, public key exchange, message delivery, and server authentication. He shows how clients can encrypt messages while servers securely communicate and verify each other. The approach provides a practical foundation for building a simple, decentralized messenger without relying on a central server.
item.description: How to create your own decentralized messenger protocol

item.title: Notes on incidents
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Notes on incidents

Sean Goedecke

6 minutes by Sean Goedecke Most incidents resolve without any action, and rushing to fix things often makes them worse. The best first step is to do nothing, take a breath, and observe. Simple fixes like disabling a feature flag usually solve the problem, but only if you know the system well enough to act decisively. Fixing incidents earns goodwill, but it is not a reliable path to lasting influence.
item.description: Notes on incidents

item.title: Growing as an engineer in a world of AI
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Growing as an engineer in a world of AI

Norberto Lopes

18 minutes by Norberto Lopes Norberto argues that leaning on AI to generate code without understanding it stunts your growth as an engineer. The learning that used to happen through struggle, repetition, and debugging is exactly what AI removes. To grow, he suggests treating AI as a thinking partner rather than an answer machine: ask why, type code out instead of pasting it, read the foundational books, and stay close to the hard conversations AI cannot join.
item.description: Growing as an engineer in a world of AI

item.title: 90% of the t distribution
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
90% of the t distribution

Kqr

3 minutes by Kqr Gosset found that using a normal distribution to calculate confidence intervals gives results that are too narrow, because it treats an estimated standard deviation as exact. He developed correction factors based on sample size to fix this. With just two data points, you can estimate a standard deviation by multiplying the difference between them by 1.3, which helps judge whether a result is truly unusual. And the most popular article from the last issue was:
item.description: 90% of the t distribution

item.title: .NET 11 performance edition
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
.NET 11 performance edition

Steven Giesel

Steven looks into several notable speed improvements that .NET 11 brings with its release. Enum comparisons are 7x faster with no memory allocations, timezone conversions are 2x faster, and GUID parsing is about 20% faster. LINQ Min and Max see big gains for smaller data types like bytes and shorts, though integers and longs show little change. Results vary by machine and setup.
item.description: .NET 11 performance edition

item.title: Multi-Tenant .NET: Shared database with schema separation
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Multi-Tenant .NET: Shared database with schema separation

Barret Blake

Barret explains how to build a multi-tenant .NET application using a shared database with a separate schema for each tenant. He shows how this approach improves data isolation while removing query filters and tenant IDs. He also discusses the key EF Core model cache issue, schema provisioning, migrations, and the trade-offs compared with other multi-tenant designs.
item.description: Multi-Tenant .NET: Shared database with schema separation

item.title: Understanding the fetch metadata HTTP headers
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Understanding the fetch metadata HTTP headers

Andrew Lock

In this post Andrew looks at the Fetch Metadata HTTP headers that have been part of browsers for several years now. He describes what each of the four headers means, when they're sent, and how you might consider using them.
item.description: Understanding the fetch metadata HTTP headers

item.title: Adding a clone method to a C# record
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Adding a clone method to a C# record

Gérald Barré

C# records provide a simple way to copy objects using the with expression, but sample with { } may not be obvious to every API user. Records also prevent you from defining your own Clone method. Gérald points out that a clean alternative is an extension method that calls with { }, giving consumers a clear and discoverable Clone() API while keeping the record’s built-in behavior intact.
item.description: Adding a clone method to a C# record

item.title: How to optimize SQL queries
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How to optimize SQL queries

Anton Martyniuk

Slow SQL queries can hurt application performance, but many problems can be fixed with a few practical techniques. Anton covers 20 ways to optimize queries, including using indexes correctly, fetching less data, simplifying joins, improving pagination, and keeping transactions short. He explains why execution plans and fresh statistics matter. The key lesson: measure first, then optimize what actually causes the slowdown. And the most popular article from the last issue was:
item.description: How to optimize SQL queries

item.title: Before You Delegate, Ask Yourself These 6 Questions
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Before You Delegate, Ask Yourself These 6 Questions

Wes Kao

(1) What does this person know? What’s new for them? (2) Why are we doing this? (3) What do they need in order to do this task? (4) What does great look like? (5) What’s the timeline and priority level? (6) What’s most likely to go wrong? What can I do to prevent this from happening?

#Management Delegation Tips
item.description: Before You Delegate, Ask Yourself These 6 Questions

item.title: The Big Management Lie: Overpromising
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Big Management Lie: Overpromising

“When managers are under pressure, and especially when they’re under pressure to retain a high performer, overpromising is one of the most common tools to reach for. The industry is rife with promises that someone will get a promotion, a new role, a large bonus, 5 more days of vacation, or any number of goodies, large or small.”

#Management Retention DifficultConversations
item.description: The Big Management Lie: Overpromising

item.title: Yes You Can Measure Engineering
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Yes You Can Measure Engineering

Jade Rubick

“I’d like to share my favorite way of measuring the value delivery of engineering organizations. It’s something I’ve used at a lot of companies. I call it the ValueSum metric.”

#Management Metrics
item.description: Yes You Can Measure Engineering

item.title: Finding Calm In Life And Work
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Finding Calm In Life And Work

Yew Jin Lim

“In a meta study involving 177 studies and more than 22,000 people, researchers found that being anxious reliably predicts worse performance on various measures, including working memory, which is the part of your mind that does the processing, the reasoning, and the problem solving.”

#Productivity Wellbeing
item.description: Finding Calm In Life And Work

item.title: Beyond “Clean Code”: Why Your Comments Matter
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Beyond “Clean Code”: Why Your Comments Matter

Tom Moertel

“To the extent that your programming language lets you express these things naturally in your logic, you should do so. But don’t contort your logic to accommodate intent and “why” information that would be easier for your audience to understand in natural language.”

#Communication CodeQuality
item.description: Beyond “Clean Code”: Why Your Comments Matter

item.title: Building An Advanced Agentic Harness
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Building An Advanced Agentic Harness

Bruno Gonçalves

“In this post we upgrade every piece of our basic harness toward that production shape, without hiding any of the mechanics behind a framework. The guiding question for the whole exercise is a simple one: How do you turn a single LLM call into a reliable system that can plan, act, recover, and prove it did the right thing?”

#DeepDive AI Agents
item.description: Building An Advanced Agentic Harness

item.title: How To Write An Effective Software Design Document
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
How To Write An Effective Software Design Document

Michael Lynch

“I’ve written design docs as a developer at Google, Microsoft, and within my own companies. The specifics vary, but the underlying principles remain the same. A design doc should articulate the hard problems you’re solving and help your teammates give you feedback. Below, I share my approach to creating effective design docs and explain what belongs in a design doc and what does not.”

#KnowledgeManagement Guide
item.description: How To Write An Effective Software Design Document

16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;margin-bottom: 16px;overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><span>Every application built on stored data performs two kinds of operations against it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A write operation records a fact, such as a new order, a changed email address, or a deleted comment. On the other hand, a read operation answers a question, such as which orders were placed this week or what should appear on a profile page. A single database on modest hardware can handle both types of operations without much trouble, and a developer need not be bothered about which operation is more common in the application’s context.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, high traffic can change things. Let’s say a page starts to load slowly. A fix is identified, which is creating an index on the column being filtered. Now, several months later, the same page is slow again under higher load. This time the fix is a cache in front of the query. A year after that, the database saturates during peak hours. This time the fix is a read replica with reporting traffic routed to it. In principle, each fix works, but each one is needed at a different time and for a different reason.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Now, let’s assume that a user updates a profile, reloads the page, but still sees the previous value. The bug does not reproduce locally, and it disappears on its own before anyone can investigate its root cause. However, this behavior can be a direct consequence of some of the other fixes. This is because each of the previous fixes placed a copy of some data somewhere other than its source. But the copy is not updated in sync with the source update. In other words, a seemingly simple fix on the read path can impact how things appear to work on the write path.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we will look at read path and write path operations and techniques in detail. Here’s what we will cover:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Why fast reads and correct writes require opposing data structures</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Precomputation and duplication, the single operation underneath every read optimization</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Two different definitions of consistency, and the bugs caused by treating them as one</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: They need specialized hardware, they consume large amounts of memory, and they add cost and delay to every request they handle.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>These traits make them hard to deploy in places where resources are limited, such as a mobile device or a service that handles heavy traffic and needs fast and low-cost responses.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>There is also a second fact that sounds backward at first. A small model can sometimes match or beat a much larger model on a specific task, even when the small model learned everything it knows from the larger one. On an intuitive level, a model trained on another model’s output would seem to inherit a ceiling rather than break through it, yet the results are different. The method that makes this work is called knowledge distillation, and it has become a standard part of how production AI systems get built.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>In this article, we will walk through the idea from the ground up. The main points we will cover are as follows:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>What distillation is, and how it differs from compression.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Why learning from a model’s output can beat learning from raw labels.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The three main methods, and which one dominates?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>What distilled models achieve in practice.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Where the method breaks down, and where it is heading next.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Distillation</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Distillation trains a new, smaller model to copy the behavior of a larger one. The setup involves two models:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The first is a large, capable model called the teacher.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The second is a smaller model called the student, which is trained to reproduce the teacher’s outputs.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Once training finishes, the student runs on its own, and the teacher steps out of the picture.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A common assumption is that the student is the teacher in compressed form. The reality, however, is different.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Compression methods such as quantization and pruning start with one model and reduce its footprint by storing its numbers at lower precision or removing parts that contribute little to the result. The model stays the same model, smaller and lighter.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Distillation, on the other hand, produces a genuinely separate model, with its own parameters and often a different design, whose goal during training is to behave like the teacher.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>One operation shrinks an existing model. The other trains a fresh one. The payoff is practical, since a small student can run inside a single service or on a phone, respond in less time, and cost far less for each request, and in some cases, it can run on the device itself without sending data elsewhere.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 justify"><span>This method is now standard practice. For example, Google’s Gemma models are built using distillation during training, drawing on a larger model in the Gemini family. The two ideas also work together in sequence. A model is often distilled first to produce a smaller capable model, then quantized to shrink that model further for a specific device.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Keeping the distinction clear matters because it affects how we understand further concepts. A compressed model carries a copy of the original inside it. A distilled model is a separate thing that was trained to act like the original, which is exactly why it can sometimes behave in ways the original would not.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>If the student only copies the teacher, why does copying work so well?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The answer is in what the teacher hands over.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Soft Labels</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Learning from a model’s output beats learning from raw data because the output carries more information than a plain answer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Standard training data gives one answer per example. An image of a cat carries the label “cat,” and the model is rewarded for producing “cat” and penalized for anything else. A teacher model offers something richer. Instead of a single answer, its output is a set of probabilities across the options, such as cat at 0.70, dog at 0.25, and fox at 0.05. That full set of probabilities is called a soft label, in contrast to the single hard label found in ordinary data.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The extra numbers carry additional information. They show that the teacher’s output ranks dog as a plausible alternative and fox as a distant one, which says something about how the categories relate to each other. Researchers sometimes call this dark knowledge, meaning the structure hidden in a model’s confidence that a bare label leaves out.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" justify"><span>During training, the student works to match this distribution. It is scored on how far its own probabilities sit from the teacher’s, and training pushes it to close that gap. In other words, the student learns the teacher’s whole pattern of confidence rather than a single right answer, and that pattern is a stronger training signal than a one-word label.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>This is the core reason distillation works as well as it does. A single correct label discards the relationships between options, and soft labels keep them.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>An early result showed the practical payoff, since a student could reach good performance from far fewer examples when trained on soft targets, because each example now carried more than a single answer. The original 2015 work added a control called temperature for exactly this purpose, where a higher temperature spreads the probabilities out and exposes more of that fine structure for the student to learn.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>With the mechanism clear, the next question is how this gets done in practice, which has more than one answer.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Methods</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Distillation comes in three main forms, and they differ in what the student copies:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Output distillation:</span></strong><span> The student matches the teacher’s final outputs, including the soft labels described above. This is the original form from 2015 and the most direct one.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Feature distillation:</span></strong><span> The student matches the teacher’s internal representations, meaning the intermediate values a model computes while processing an input, before it settles on a final answer. The aim is a similar internal picture, not only a similar output. Google’s EmbeddingGemma is trained this way, learning to produce internal representations close to those of a larger Gemini model.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Synthetic data distillation: </span></strong><span>The teacher generates a dataset of examples, and the student is fine-tuned on that dataset the same way it would be trained on any ordinary data. Stanford’s Alpaca was an early case, fine-tuned on examples produced by an existing large model to improve how well it followed instructions.</span></p></li></ul><div justify"><span>The third form has become the most common approach in practice, and part of the reason comes down to access.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Many strong models are reachable only through an interface that returns text, with their internal values and probabilities kept private. When those internals are out of reach, generating data is the route that still works.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The three forms also differ in what they require. Output distillation needs the teacher’s probabilities, feature distillation needs access to its internal values, and synthetic data distillation needs only the text the teacher produces, which is why it travels the furthest across closed models.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>These methods can also be combined. A single training run might use a generated dataset alongside soft labels, and newer methods mix teacher and student generation during training.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>These methods are not only theoretical. The next section shows what they produce.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Results</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The results in practice are strong, with one important qualifier.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A clear example came in early 2025 from a lab called DeepSeek. It used a large reasoning model to generate a set of training examples, then fine-tuned several existing smaller models on those examples. One result stood out.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A 7-billion-parameter student scored higher than a 32-billion-parameter model on a competition mathematics benchmark, even though it was produced by plain fine-tuning on the larger model’s outputs. The released family of distilled models ran from 1.5 billion parameters up to 70 billion, and the smaller ones were compact enough to run on a single graphics card, which is part of why the release drew so much attention. The practical effect was that strong performance on these narrow tasks became something a small team could run locally and cheaply, rather than only through a large hosted model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The qualifier matters as much as the headline.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>These wins tend to appear on narrow, well-defined tasks such as mathematics and code. On those tasks, a small distilled model can perform at a level its size would not suggest. Across broader measures of general knowledge, the same small models still trail the larger ones. For example, a model can become excellent at competition mathematics through distillation while remaining weaker at wide-ranging questions about the world. Therefore, a claim that a small model beats a large one is usually true in a specific, narrow sense.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: justify"><span>If the results are this good, the natural question is where the method falls short, which the next section takes on directly.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Limits</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Distillation has clear limits, and they matter when deciding whether it fits a given problem.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>A ceiling effect from the teacher:</span></strong><span> A student trained on a teacher’s output tends to stay at or below the teacher’s level on the kind of data they saw. When the teacher produces a wrong answer, the student learns that wrong answer along with the right ones. The teacher’s quality sets the bar, which makes the choice of teacher one of the most consequential decisions in the process.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>A wider gap can hurt: </span></strong><span>A larger, stronger teacher does not always produce a better student. When the gap between teacher and student is very wide, transfer can degrade, because the student has too little capacity to absorb everything that a much larger model expresses. Research on this capacity gap has found that the strongest available teacher is sometimes a poor choice. A set of methods exists to bridge wide gaps by adding a middle step, where the teacher trains a mid-sized model and that model trains the small student, so each handoff spans a smaller distance.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Architecture can outweigh size:</span></strong><span> The design of the base model can matter more than its parameter count. In one study, a 32-billion-parameter student outperformed a 70-billion-parameter student on the same task, because the smaller one was built on a stronger base architecture. Size alone is a weak predictor of how well distillation will go.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>The teacher can pass on more than the task:</span></strong><span> In a 2025 study later published in Nature, a teacher model with a particular trait, a tendency to favor owls, was used to generate training data made up only of number sequences. A student trained on those numbers picked up the same preference for owls, even after the data was filtered to remove any visible trace of the trait. The same effect appeared with more serious behaviors, and it occurred only when the teacher and student shared the same base model. The takeaway is that distillation can carry across more than the task being taught, and that filtering the visible data is sometimes too coarse to stop it.</span></p></li></ul><div justify"><span>These limits set the boundaries, and within them, the method keeps advancing. The next section covers where it is heading.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Automation</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The newest direction in distillation reduces the manual effort by automating the whole process.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>In this setup, the large model runs the full loop on its own. It generates training data, fine-tunes the student, evaluates the student against a held-out set of examples it also generates, and repeats the cycle, adjusting what it produces until the student stops improving. The human role shrinks to defining the task and the success criteria at the start, with a final check on real data at the end.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" justify"><span>Recent work in 2026 applied this to a detection task and found that it worked well, with one finding worth keeping in mind.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The choice of teacher model had a large effect on the outcome. Different teachers, given the same loop and the same student, produced students of noticeably different quality. So automation removes manual effort while making the initial choice of teacher more consequential, since that choice now drives an entire self-running process rather than a single training pass.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The same loop also points toward less hand-built pipeline work over time, as more of the data generation and evaluation moves to the model itself. For a team, the appeal is building a small, task-specific model without assembling a large hand-labeled dataset first, since the teacher supplies both the training examples and the data used to score them.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Distillation is a method for training a small, deployable model to copy the behavior of a large, expensive one. It produces a separate model rather than a compressed version of the original, and that distinction explains most of how it behaves.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>It works because a model’s output carries more information than a plain label, in the form of soft labels that show a full pattern of confidence across the options.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>In practice, the most common form has the teacher generate a training set that the student learns from, and the results can be strong, though usually on narrow tasks.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The limits are real:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The teacher sets a ceiling,</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>A wider size gap can hurt rather than help,</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Architecture can outweigh size</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The process can carry across traits that were never intended.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Taken together, distillation tends to be a good fit when the task is well defined and a capable teacher is available, and a weaker fit when the goal is broad, open-ended capability.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><strong><span>References:</span></strong></p><ul rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Why does sending a model a 100K-word prompt cost so much more than sending it a short one, even when the model and the hardware stay the same?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A key part of the answer lies in a block of working memory called the KV cache.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>This memory is built up while the model generates a response. It is separate from the knowledge stored in the model’s weights, and it holds the key and value vectors computed for every token of the input. The cache grows with every token, and in a long context, it can take up significant space on the GPU.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>For example,  for a 70-billion-parameter model at a context of 128,000 tokens, it comes to roughly 40 gigabytes, a serious amount of GPU memory that grows with every In this article, we will learn how LLMs use memory, how it gets expensive, and how to fix it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><em><span>Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Recomputation</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Let us start with the work a model does to produce one token.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>To choose the next word, it runs an attention step, where the newest token compares itself against every token that came before it. This comparison uses two vectors for each earlier token, a key and a value, which are simply the numerical summaries the model computes for that token inside each layer. A model that rebuilt the key and value for every earlier token at every step would watch the work per token climb as the input grows. Such a repetition is pure waste, because those keys and values stay the same once a token has been processed.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The KV cache removes the waste by storing those key and value vectors the first time they are computed. On the next step, the model computes the key and value for only the new token and reads the rest straight from the cache.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" justify"><span>Overall, this is a great solution. However, caching fixes the speed problem while creating a new one. The cache now has to be read on every step, and this turns out to be the real source of increasing cost.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>One detail worth understanding here is that the cache holds vectors rather than the original text. It also explains out-of-memory errors that look puzzling when the model itself fits with room to spare.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Decoding</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Generation of tokens runs in two phases, and they stress the hardware in different ways:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The first phase is prefill, where the model reads the entire input at once. It processes all of the input tokens in parallel and builds their key and value vectors into the cache in a single pass. Prefill keeps the GPU’s math units busy, so we call it compute-bound, meaning the limit is how fast the chip can do arithmetic.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The second phase is decoding, where the model produces the output one token at a time. Each new token runs an attention step against the whole cache, which means the model reads every stored key and value out of GPU memory before it can emit the next token. It repeats that read for every token it produces. The limit here is how fast the cache can move from memory into the compute units, so we call decoding memory-bound.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" justify"><span>The expense of long-context generation comes less from holding the cache and more from sweeping through all of it on every single token.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A larger cache means more data crossing the memory bus per token, which shows up directly as slower and costlier generation. It also explains why a request can run slowly even when it fits in memory comfortably.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>If the cost tracks how much of the cache we read each step, then the size of the cache is the next thing to understand clearly.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Scaling</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The cache size is the product of a handful of numbers:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>A factor of two covers the key and the value.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Layers count because each layer keeps its own cache.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Key-value heads set how many sets each layer stores.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Head dimension is the size of each of those vectors.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Bytes per number is the space one stored value takes.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Tokens are the context length, with one entry each.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Batch size is the number of requests served at once.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>To summarize, the cache size equals 2 times layers times key-value heads times head dimension times bytes per number times tokens times batch size.</span></p><div justify"><span>Two things that should be noted here are as follows:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The cache grows in a straight line with the token count, so doubling the context doubles the cache</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>It grows the same way with the batch size, so serving more users at once scales it just as fast.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>As an approximate example, a Llama 3 70B model has 80 layers, 8 key-value heads, a head dimension of 128, and stores each number in 2 bytes. At a context of 128,000 tokens for a single request, those numbers multiply out to roughly 40 gigabytes, which is why a single long request can fill most of an 80-gigabyte card on its own.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Let us now look at the optimization techniques that help an LLM manage the memory aspects. Each of these techniques tries to push against a specific number.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Attention</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The first two techniques change how attention itself is built, which means a model is committed to them during training. Both shrink the footprint of each token in the cache.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Grouped-query attention goes after the key-value head count. In a standard attention layer, every query head carries its own key and value head, so a model with 64 query heads stores 64 sets of keys and values. Grouped-query attention lets several query heads share one key-value head, which drops the number of stored sets sharply. For example, Llama 2 and 3 at 70B and Mistral 7B share down to 8 key-value heads, which cuts the cache by roughly eightfold against full multi-head attention. This is why a recent 70B model can hold a smaller cache than an older 7B one.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>There is a more aggressive version called multi-query attention, where every query head shares a single key-value head. It saves the most memory of any head-sharing scheme. However, pushed that far, quality tends to drop, and training grows unstable, so most setups settle on the grouped middle ground as the better trade.</span></p><div justify"><span>The second attack keeps the heads and compresses what each one stores.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Multi-head latent attention, introduced in the DeepSeek models, projects the keys and values down into a smaller latent representation before caching them, then expands them back when they are read. The savings are large. DeepSeek-V3 holds around 70 kilobytes per token, where comparable grouped-query models sit between 192 and 328. The cost lies in serving, since the compression adds work on every read and pairs awkwardly with some standard attention implementations, so it tends to pay off most once models and contexts grow large enough that cache traffic dominates.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>As mentioned, head-sharing and latent attention both require control over the architecture, so they help when we are choosing or training a model. The next attacks work on a model we already have in hand.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Quantization</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Quantization goes after the bytes per number.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The keys and values are usually stored at 16 bits each, and quantization rounds them to a smaller format such as 8 bits or 4 bits. Since the bytes-per-number term sits right there in the equation, moving from 16 bits to 8 halves the whole cache, and going to 4 bits halves it again. The appeal is that this applies to a model we already have and skips retraining entirely.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The quality cost depends on how far we push it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Eight-bit storage often costs well under a percent of accuracy, which puts it within the noise for most workloads. Four-bit storage saves more and starts to show measurable losses on demanding tasks such as multi-needle retrieval, where the model has to pull several specific facts out of a long context.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Specialized methods beat plain rounding because a few numbers in the cache deserve more precision than the rest, though plain rounding already captures most of the gain.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Eviction</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Eviction goes after the token count by dropping entries that the model is unlikely to need.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The common approach keeps a window of the most recent tokens, since recent context usually matters most, along with a few tokens from the very start of the sequence. Those opening tokens turn out to play an outsized role. They absorb a large share of attention regardless of what they actually say, acting as anchors that keep the model’s output stable.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: justify"><span>The trouble with eviction is structural.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Whether a token matters depends on a question that has yet to arrive. A token we drop now can be exactly the one a later part of the generation needs, and once it is gone, the model generates as though that token had been absent the whole time. This shows up on retrieval tasks, where an aggressively trimmed cache handles a casual chat well and then misses a fact buried in the middle of a long document.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>More refined schemes score each token’s importance and try to predict which ones are safe to drop, which helps, though the core problem remains.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Serving</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Even with the contents of the cache fixed, the way a serving system manages memory leaves a lot on the table, and two techniques help.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The first is paged attention.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Older serving systems reserved one large contiguous block per request, sized for the longest output it might produce. Most requests finished well short of that, leaving the reserved space idle, and the fragmentation added up. However, paged attention borrows an idea from operating systems, which break memory into small fixed-size pages and hand them out on demand. The cache gets split into small blocks that can live anywhere in memory, tracked by a lookup table that maps each request to its blocks. The result is that systems that wasted 60 to 80 percent of cache memory to fragmentation dropped that figure below 4 percent, and throughput climbed by two to three times, all from packing the same data more tightly.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table justify"><span>The second technique results from the first. Since the cache lives in shareable blocks, two requests that begin with the same text can point at the same physical blocks while each holds its own private continuation. This is the foundation of prefix caching, and the productized version that the major APIs call prompt caching.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The win is large for any workload that repeats a prefix, such as an agent that sends the same multi-thousand-token system prompt on every call. OpenAI and Anthropic both report cost and latency reductions of 50 to 90 percent on cache hits, with cached tokens billed at a fraction of fresh ones.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>However, one thing to note is that sharing cached state across users has opened timing side-channels that can leak information about other people’s prompts, an active concern we will leave aside here.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Tradeoffs</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The techniques we’ve looked at look alike in how much memory they save and differ widely in what they ask for in return.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Some are close to free. For example:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Grouped-query attention costs very little quality and has become the safe default, which is why nearly every current model ships with it.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Paged attention and prefix caching barely touch quality, since they change how the cache is stored and shared rather than what it contains.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Other techniques require more. For example:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Quantization is cheap at 8 bits and grows risky as we push toward 4 and below, so the right setting depends on how sensitive the task is.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Latent attention saves most of the architectural options and asks for real engineering effort to serve well.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Eviction frees a large amount of memory and can also lose information that the generation later needs, which makes it a genuine gamble rather than a clean win.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table They earn their place in a long context and high concurrency, where the cache grows into the dominant cost. The right mix follows the workload, with agent loops leaning on reuse and long-document retrieval leaning away from eviction.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The cost of long-context inference comes down to one cache, sized by one short equation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Since decoding reads the whole cache on every token, the cache is a bandwidth cost as much as a storage one, which is why shrinking it speeds things up. Every optimization we covered deals with a specific aspect of the overall equation or trims the waste around it.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Grouped query and latent attention reduce what each token costs.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Quantization stores each number in fewer bits.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Eviction keeps fewer tokens.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Paged attention and prefix caching manage and share the cache more efficiently.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: item.ns0:encoded:
Dealing With Surprising Human Emotions: Desk Moves

Lara Hogan

“Desk moves are my favorite example of why managers should understand the brain science behind why people react they way they do, in otherwise not-that-emotional circumstances.”

#Management ChangeManagement

item.title: Engineering Management After The Cost Of Code Collapsed
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Engineering Management After The Cost Of Code Collapsed

Karim Jedda

“I still hear and read what I call the "old rules" repeated over and over: a director should not spend time coding, good work takes time, protect the team from the business, get consensus before you commit, etc...” Karim started checking each rule against the assumption underneath it after the introduction of LLMs in his org.

#Management AI
item.description: Engineering Management After The Cost Of Code Collapsed

item.title: The Conductor Developer
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Conductor Developer

Rachel Laycock

“A great conductor is first and foremost a great musician. They could play the instruments themselves. That’s not why they’re standing on the podium. Their value comes from understanding the whole score. The orchestra doesn’t need the conductor because the musicians aren’t talented enough. It needs the conductor because someone has to hold the whole system in their head. Increasingly, I think that’s what great software developers are doing.”

#Leadership CareerGrowth
item.description: The Conductor Developer

item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
My Agentic Coding Setup, July 2026

Domenic Denicola

“Things are changing very fast, and I have no illusions that this will be a timeless nugget of wisdom. But talking to some friends and scrolling through X posts, it does seem that I might have some techniques in play that are not widespread.”

#DevEx AI Agents
item.description: My Agentic Coding Setup, July 2026

item.title: Work Loudly
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Work Loudly

Ben Balter

“In remote work, visibility isn't ambient anymore. If your work only shows up at the end - or only in your head and DMs—you make it harder for people to help, harder for managers to advocate for you, and easier for the org to miss your impact.” Ben shares his approach to working loudly.

#Communication CareerGrowth Remote
item.description: Work Loudly

item.title: The Bedrock of Software Design
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Bedrock of Software Design

Alex Fedoseev

“Nothing has influenced the way I design software more than algebraic data types. It sounds overly academic—the kind of term that makes people roll their eyes or scares them away altogether. But honestly, it only sounds scary. The idea itself is quite simple, and learning it showed me a fundamentally better way to build software.”

#DeepDive Architecture CodeQuality
item.description: The Bedrock of Software Design

item.title: Every Byte Matters
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Every Byte Matters

Farid Zakaria

Farid argues that classic analysis isn't enough. The size of your data matters as much as your algorithm. CPUs pull memory in 64-byte "cache lines," so how tightly your data packs into those lines impacts speed.

#DeepDive Architecture Performance
item.description: Every Byte Matters

rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In June 2025, security researchers at Aim Security demonstrated that a single email could cause Microsoft 365 Copilot to retrieve a company’s internal files and transmit them to an external server, with no user interaction.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The email contained ordinary text and exploited no software flaw. Copilot’s output was driven by hidden instructions in the email together with the user’s actual request, and the system applied no distinction between the two. Microsoft closed the specific path within days and reported that customers were unaffected.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But this incident sheds interesting light on how language models process text. The vulnerability was named EchoLeak, assigned CVE-2025-32711, and it serves as a useful study to understand the landscape of LLM security.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static"
