position on the spectrum was largely determined by the infrastructure it already had.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>DoorDash already had a knowledge graph that classical retrieval could exploit, so the cheapest gain came from making the graph richer and teaching queries how to talk to it.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Instacart had specialized query-understanding models that were hard to maintain, so the biggest win came from consolidation under a unified LLM strategy.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Uber Eats already had two-tower embedding infrastructure running per vertical, so the natural next step was swapping in a fine-tuned LLM as the shared backbone, allowing one model to handle every vertical and every language.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The lesson would be that before asking which LLM to use for some task, the better question is where in an existing stack an LLM would actually help.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Three of the largest food delivery companies rebuilt search around LLMs in the same window of time, with overlapping research literature and similar production constraints, and they arrived at three completely distinct architectures.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The reason food search was a good place to investigate this is that it breaks classical keyword retrieval in many ways simultaneously. Subjective queries (something healthy for a rainy evening), long-tail traffic, multilingual catalogs, and compound constraints all sit in the same search bar.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The three approaches each represent a different setting:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>DoorDash uses LLMs offline to enrich a knowledge graph, while classical retrieval still drives the runtime.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Instacart uses LLMs at the query understanding layer, with fine-tuned smaller models handling tail queries in the hot path.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Uber Eats fine-tuned a Qwen LLM into the embedding backbone of two-tower retrieval, so every query and every document gets an LLM-derived vector.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Each company’s position on this spectrum traces back to the infrastructure it already had, which is why the depth-of-integration question matters more than the model choice.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Three universal tradeoffs survived every architecture.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Hybrid systems are the default everywhere. Classical retrieval, knowledge graphs, and ANN indexes still do most of the work.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>World knowledge from a pre-trained model is just a head start. Domain context still has to be injected somewhere, through RAG, fine-tuning, or both.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Guardrails are an important part of every production LLM system. Constrained vocabularies, similarity filters, and taxonomy enforcement quietly determine whether outputs stay aligned with the catalog.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: item.title: Mission To Metrics
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Mission To Metrics

Annie Zhou

“Mission to Metrics is a written cascade, running from why the org exists down to the numbers that measure whether it’s getting there. Every team’s plan is a more detailed version of one slice of the layer above. Every metric traces back to the mission. Once it’s written, anyone in the org can read the page and understand how their work connects to the company mission.”

#Leadership Management Metrics
item.description: Mission To Metrics

item.title: The Vital Few
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Vital Few

Mike Fisher

“Stewardship is the actual work. It means giving your strongest people air cover, not just assignments. It means defending their focus from the steady drizzle of interruptions that drifts toward competence. It means offering them growth rather than merely more volume, and fighting the reflex to drop the next critical thing on the proven desk simply because it is proven.”

#Leadership Management Retention
item.description: The Vital Few

item.title: Make No Assumptions
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Make No Assumptions

Will Larson

“When that architect leaves, they are replaced by someone who aspires to operate in the same code layer, but simply cannot because they lack enough context to do so. As a result, that new replacement creates a new code layer, despite not intending to. If the team runs through a handful of folks as the new team leads struggle, it’s easy to end up with a complex code horizon very quickly.”

#Leadership AI CodeReview
item.description: Make No Assumptions

item.title: The State Of AI Impact In Engineering: Q2 2026
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The State Of AI Impact In Engineering: Q2 2026

Justin Reock

“Engineering leaders are now under immense pressure to justify exponentially-increasing AI budgets. The data from our Q2 report reveals that while AI is delivering objective gains in velocity, those gains are highly uneven.”

#Survey AI IndustryTrends
item.description: The State Of AI Impact In Engineering: Q2 2026

item.title: Building Ask DoorDash: A Platform For Building and Evolving Agents
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Building Ask DoorDash: A Platform For Building and Evolving Agents

“We built Ask DoorDash on a common platform that lets domain teams build and evolve their agents without rebuilding the systems beneath them. We judged the platform by two practical outcomes: how quickly teams could add features and domains, and how quickly they could evaluate and release improvements to cost, quality, and latency.”

#Architecture PlatformEng Agents
item.description: Building Ask DoorDash: A Platform For Building and Evolving Agents

item.title: The New Rules Of Context Engineering For Claude 5 Models
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The New Rules Of Context Engineering For Claude 5 Models

Thariq Shihipar

“Here’s what we’ve learned about prompting this new class of models, and how you can utilize it to update your context engineering. We’ve put these best practices in claude doctor, use the command /doctor in Claude Code to rightsize your skills, and CLAUDE.md files.”

#Guide AI
item.description: The New Rules Of Context Engineering For Claude 5 Models

item.title: The Git History Command Deserves More Attention
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Git History Command Deserves More Attention

Lalit Maganti

"Working with lots of changes in parallel on git can be painful. You end up juggling branches and commits, and running scary rebase -i commands that can leave your tree in a half-broken state if you so much as sneeze.”

#Git

Physical AI</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Language models are great at predicting the next token, but they do not understand the physical world. They cannot tell you how a shirt sleeve folds, or what a glass of water looks like the moment it tips over. A robot or a self-driving car needs that kind of understanding, but it cannot get it from text.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That is what a world model provides. Instead of predicting the next word, it understands the world and can predict the next state given the current state of the world and an action. It can generate realistic, physically plausible video, reason about motion and cause and effect, and produce the action data a robot needs to learn.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>World models are extremely useful because you can use them to create training data for situations that are slow, expensive, or dangerous to capture in the real world.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table Healthcare, autonomous vehicles, quantum, and more specialized applications</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The lineup keeps going. Alpamayo is an open model family for reasoning-based self-driving. Like GR00T, it uses Cosmos as its reasoning backbone, so the same physical-AI foundation that powers robots also lets a car work through road situations it was never trained on. It also exposes the chain of cause and effect behind each decision, which developers can inspect and build on. BioNeMo brings open models to biology and drug discovery, and the BioNeMo Agent Toolkit lets developers build autonomous agents for life sciences work. Ising gives quantum computer builders, operators, and developers the AI tools needed to scale devices to fault tolerance. Earth-2 is a family of open models, libraries, and frameworks that makes professional-grade weather and climate AI available to anyone. On top of these, NVIDIA offers open models for production use: safety models that filter unsafe content, speech models for voice, and vision models for images.</span></p><div style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Taken together, this powerful ecosystem changes how the community can advance and build. The rest of the article looks at how NVIDIA builds these models, how the team is able to move fast, and what they have learned.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>How the Models Are Built to Be Frontier and Fast</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It is often a challenge to build a model that is both fast and capable. Capable models are usually larger, which makes them slower to train and to answer questions. NVIDIA’s answer is to chase the frontier and speed at the same time. Bryan put it this way: “the fastest model is the smartest model.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>While this may sound like a slogan, it has a real insight. A faster model can be trained on more data in the same amount of time. It can be post-trained across more environments. Once deployed, it can think for longer on a hard problem at the same cost. So speed translates into capability and compounds at every stage.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Given this strategy, NVIDIA designs its models with a focus on efficiency and speed. The following design choices are what make these models both fast and capable. The first two make the model faster and more efficient. The last one makes it more capable.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>1. The hybrid architecture</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Most well-known models are built almost entirely on the Transformer’s attention mechanism. Attention lets every token in the input look at every other token, which is powerful for capturing relationships but expensive. The cost grows with the square of the input length, so doubling the input roughly quadruples the work. The model has to keep every earlier token in memory as it runs. On very long inputs, that gets slow and costly.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The other main class is the state space model, and Mamba is its best-known example. Instead of comparing every token with every other one, a Mamba layer reads the sequence once and compresses everything it has seen into a fixed-size memory. That makes it cheap: the cost grows linearly with length, and the memory stays constant no matter how long the input. The tradeoff is that a fixed-size memory cannot keep every detail, so Mamba is weaker at recalling one exact fact buried far back.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" sequence. Attention can always go back and find an exact fact. Put together, they are smarter than either one alone. NVIDIA published this hybrid result in 2024, and other labs, including the teams behind Qwen and Kimi, have since moved in the same direction.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>2. Co-designing the GPU and the model</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The second choice is where NVIDIA’s two businesses meet. Its larger models are pretrained in a 4-bit number format called NVFP4, meaning most of the math during training uses just four bits per value. Fewer bits means less memory and less data to move, so the math runs faster and on less power.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Note that four bits is very little precision. Most teams train in higher precision and only shrink the model afterward, which loses accuracy. NVIDIA trained in 4 bits from the first step because it knew its next GPU generation, Blackwell, was being built with fast 4-bit hardware. The model and the chip were designed for each other.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The VP described the mindset behind it. Moore’s law is no longer giving easy gains every generation, so progress has to come from designing the model and the hardware together. The team only attempted 4-bit pretraining because it believed the result was possible. In his words, the first step to inventing something amazing is believing that you can.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>3. Post-training: learning from experience</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With those efficiency choices in place, post-training is where the model gains its capability.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The post-training recipe itself is what most other teams converged to. It starts with supervised fine-tuning, where the model learns from curated examples of good answers and picks up the format and behavior expected of it. Then it switches to reinforcement learning, where the model practices on real tasks and is rewarded for reaching the right outcome. Instead of learning from examples, it learns from its own attempts.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Scaling up this reinforcement learning stage has been shown to improve a model’s capability significantly. Here NVIDIA’s efficiency focus pays off again. Because its models are cheaper to run, it can scale RL at a lower cost, letting the model practice across many environments in parallel and learn from over a million rollouts.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is where the VP placed the real bottleneck for better models. Not data or compute. The diversity of these training environments. The more varied the situations a model practices in, the more capable it becomes, because that is where it gains real problem-solving experience.</span></p><div style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So far we have looked at design decisions to build a model and what is involved to train a single frontier model. But how do they build so many models, and keep improving them so quickly?</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>One Unified Foundation</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Building strong models in one domain is hard. Building them across language, video, robotics, vehicles, and biology needs huge engineering and compute resources. NVIDIA’s approach is to identify a reusable foundation, build it once, and reuse it across different efforts.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The VP traced this back to CUDA, the software layer that made NVIDIA’s GPUs programmable. The “U” stands for Unified, and he called it the most important letter. The idea is to build one foundation and run everything on top of it, rather than maintaining many separate stacks.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The same instinct shapes the models. The hybrid architecture from the last section is not rebuilt for each model. The same backbone scales across all three Nemotron sizes. Whole components cross between efforts too. Cosmos Reason, the model built to reason about the physical world, was reused as the reasoning core inside NVIDIA’s Isaac GR00T foundation model, so the robotics team did not have to build that part from scratch. The alternative, ten parallel efforts each reinventing the same pieces, would spread people and compute too thin. According to Bryan, NVIDIA tries to be as lazy as possible, because that is how it gets the most out of limited resources.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The other reason the team is so productive and iterates quickly is cultural. NVIDIA is mostly not top-down; it is a company of volunteers, where teams choose what to work on, and unification happens through invitation rather than control. The culture of collaboration is that if teams work with each other and get more done, they will get more resources than if they each go alone. When everyone shares that belief, a small group can produce a lot.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Open is More Than Just Releasing Weights</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>You may have heard a lot about open models. Several AI labs released capable models. You can download the weights and use them. But that is not truly an open model. This is where NVIDIA’s approach really separates it from the other labs. As Bryan puts it, Nemotron is not just a model. It is also the data, the tools, the training recipes, and the ideas published in the papers. The finished weights are just the last step.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 learning environments, and the recipes needed to reproduce the work. A team can not only run the model, but also see how it was built and train their own version.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The same is true for robotics and self-driving cars, where developers can use open source simulation and learning frameworks, datasets to train and evaluate the model performance before deployment.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Releasing data at this scale is unusual. It is a scary thing for a company to do. NVIDIA does it anyway, and even shares clever building blocks like synthetic “persona” data that is statistically realistic but fully private, so a model can learn about the world without memorizing real people.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>You can see this in what the community has done with it. NVIDIA’s open data and models have spawned a large set of community fine-tunes and derivatives. One of its robotics datasets became one of the most-downloaded datasets on Hugging Face. Many variants of its Nemotron models have millions of downloads each, and the Nemotron family recently crossed 100M in total. You cannot build like that from the weights alone.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Why a Chip Company Gives It All Away</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>You may think releasing open models sounds great. But why would a company that sells GPUs give away the AI that runs on them?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Bryan shared two reasons. The first is that NVIDIA needs to understand AI deeply to build the right hardware for it. To design future chips, you have to know where AI is going. The best way to really know is to build models yourself and put them in front of real users. A model kept private is easy to fool yourself about, so releasing it openly keeps the work honest and keeps NVIDIA’s researchers connected to the wider community they learn from. With open models being such a hot topic, the real value is in enabling developers to post-train these models themselves at a fraction of the cost.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The second reason is about the business. NVIDIA grows whenever AI grows. Its goal is to support the ecosystem, not to compete with the companies building on top of it. Every team that adopts open models and builds its own AI can become a future customer for compute. So the company would rather hand the ecosystem the models and let the world’s demand for AI pull its business forward.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/e5bd88bc-4365-4f9d-b48b-35d630232e46?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;">Business grows as models become open</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There is also a side benefit: safety. Open technology tends to be safer because more people can inspect it and find problems, the way the open internet is hardened by everyone who uses it.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>What NVIDIA Has Learned Shipping Open Models</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Shipping this many models in public teaches lessons that closed labs never face. Bryan shared several valuable lessons.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;">Four lessons from building and shipping open models</figcaption></figure></div><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);"><strong><span>1. The program matters more than any single release</span></strong></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In a field moving this fast, every model is obsolete before it ships. So no single release is the point. What earns trust is a steady, sustained program. When the community believes a model line is here to stay, it pays attention to each new release instead of treating it as a one-off.</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);"><strong><span>2. Make it easy for developers</span></strong></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A clean launch is the result of getting a hundred small things right, from licensing to documentation to ready-to-run examples. The VP admitted this is the unglamorous part. Listening to community feedback and smoothing that first-run experience is what turns a download into lasting use.</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);"><strong><span>3. Pick a license the community trusts</span></strong></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>NVIDIA moved away from its own homegrown licenses to OpenMDW, a community license from the Linux Foundation built specifically for open AI. Using a shared, purpose-built license removes friction and signals that the models are meant to be used freely.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>What’s Next</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The direction from here is to open even earlier. Rather than build a model privately and post it when it is done, NVIDIA wants to bring collaborators in sooner, since it plans to open everything anyway. The aim is to let partners shape the models while they are still being built. To make this happen, NVIDIA formed the Nemotron and Cosmos Coalitions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What stands out most is the conviction that this is a long-term commitment, not a phase. The VP pointed to CUDA, which took more than a decade before the rest of the world understood why it mattered. NVIDIA stuck with it, and it became the foundation of the company.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>He expects open models to follow the same path. As he put it, this is not a science project, and it is not charity. It is how NVIDIA moves itself forward into the future.</span></p></div></div><div class="postscript-placeholder" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;font-size: 16px;line-height: item.title: The depth-first search pattern: Exploring trees and graphs
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
The depth-first search pattern: Exploring trees and graphs

Franco Fernando

15 minutes by Franco Fernando Depth-first search is a recursion pattern for exploring trees, graphs, and matrices. It works by going as deep as possible along one path before backtracking and trying another. To avoid infinite loops in graphs, you track visited nodes and skip them on future visits. Depth-first search fits problems where you need to find paths, check reachability, or explore all possibilities through a structure.
item.description: The depth-first search pattern: Exploring trees and graphs

item.title: Everyone should know SIMD
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Everyone should know SIMD

Mitchell Hashimoto

11 minutes by Mitchell Hashimoto SIMD lets a CPU process multiple values at once instead of one at a time, turning slow byte-by-byte loops into chunk-based operations that run 4x to 16x faster. Despite its reputation for complexity, common SIMD code follows the same five steps every time: broadcast constants, loop over chunks, operate on all values at once, reduce the result, then handle leftovers with a normal loop. Once you learn that pattern, writing SIMD is nearly as simple as writing a regular loop.
item.description: Everyone should know SIMD

item.title: htop explained
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
htop explained

Pēteris Ņikiforovs

43 minutes by Pēteris Ņikiforovs Linux tools like htop and top expose a lot of system data, and Pēteris walks through what each number and column actually means. Load average is not simply CPU usage — it counts all running and waiting processes, including those stuck on disk or network. Memory columns like VIRT and RES can be misleading, since virtual memory includes mapped but unused space. Pēteris also covers process states, signals, niceness, scheduling, and what each background service on a fresh Linux server actually does.
item.description: htop explained

item.title: In-house LLM serving at Netflix
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
In-house LLM serving at Netflix

Netflix Technology Blog

12 minutes by Netflix Technology Blog Netflix runs its own LLM serving stack on top of vLLM and NVIDIA Triton, integrated into existing production infrastructure rather than a separate system. Key decisions around engine choice, model packaging, API design, and deployment strategies each revealed unexpected trade-offs only under real production load. A notable example is constrained decoding, where per-request CPU processing caused latency to grow linearly with batch size until a rewrite using vLLM V1's batch-level API and C++ solved the bottleneck. item.description: In-house LLM serving at Netflix

item.title: operation.
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
operation.

Appaji C

9 minutes by Appaji C A fake recruiter on LinkedIn sent Appaji a Python developer job offer with a take-home coding test hidden inside a zip file. The project looked clean at first, but running a simple directory listing revealed pre-loaded Git hooks designed to silently download and execute malicious scripts the moment any Git command ran. The scripts then installed Node.js in the background and ran obfuscated code targeting crypto wallets, with unique tracking IDs assigned to each victim. item.title: Building a database in a text file — why async is not enough
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Building a database in a text file — why async is not enough

Yegor Sychev

Async code doesn't block threads, but it doesn't protect shared data either. Yegor shows the problem by building a simple file-based storage where 20 parallel writes cause crashes and data loss, because each task reads the same file, then tries to overwrite it. The fix requires explicit synchronization, which the next part of the series covers using SemaphoreSlim.
item.description: Building a database in a text file — why async is not enough

item.title: TimeProvider and the end of untestable DateTime.Now
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
TimeProvider and the end of untestable DateTime.Now

Maarten Balliauw

Before .NET 8, every team solved the same problem differently: wrapping DateTime.Now in a custom interface so tests could control the clock. TimeProvider is the standard replacement that ships with .NET 8, so no more reinventing this. Maarten suggests using TimeProvider.System in production and FakeTimeProvider in tests. The fake lets you pin the clock to a specific moment and call Advance() to move time forward instantly, making cache expiry, retries, and timer callbacks fully testable without any waiting.
item.description: TimeProvider and the end of untestable DateTime.Now

item.title: Multi-Tenant .NET: Shared database with partitions
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Multi-Tenant .NET: Shared database with partitions

Barret Blake

Multi-tenancy means many customers share one app and one database. A tenant ID column separates their data, and EF Core global query filters automatically add a WHERE clause to every query so each tenant only sees their own records. SQL Server table partitioning then physically groups each tenant's rows together, and because the filter already targets the partition column, the database skips irrelevant partitions entirely. Partitioning speeds things up but does not replace the query filter as the actual security boundary.
item.description: Multi-Tenant .NET: Shared database with partitions

item.title: Creating dual use Windows GUI and console applications
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Creating dual use Windows GUI and console applications

Rick Strahl

Rick argues that building a Windows app that works as both a GUI and a command line tool is tricky because Windows forces you to choose one mode at compile time. He points out three approaches exist: a GUI app that attaches to a console, a console app that launches a GUI, and two separate programs sharing the same code. Each has a flaw, either messy console output, a brief terminal window flash, or the overhead of maintaining two projects. For most serious tools, separate executables offer the cleanest solution despite the extra setup.
item.description: Creating dual use Windows GUI and console applications

item.title: How to prevent duplicate API requests in .NET
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How to prevent duplicate API requests in .NET

Yohan Malshika

Duplicate API requests happen more often than expected, caused by things like double clicks, network retries, or background jobs. Without proper handling, this leads to serious problems like double payments or corrupted data. Idempotency ensures that no matter how many times the same request is sent, the result stays the same. Think of it like an ATM that only processes one withdrawal even if the request is sent twice. And the most popular article from the last issue was:

I want my tools to be invisible.”

item.title: Prefactoring: Clear The Way For Your New Feature
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Prefactoring: Clear The Way For Your New Feature

Rahul Singal

“Prefactoring (short for "preparatory refactoring") is the practice of reworking existing code to make it more suitable for an upcoming change before you actually implement the new functionality. Instead of cleaning up code as an afterthought or trying to force a new feature into an incompatible structure, you restructure the codebase first.”

#Testing Guide
item.description: Prefactoring: Clear The Way For Your New Feature

Everyone Should Know SIMD

Mitchell Hashimoto

“SIMD has a reputation for being complex. I've met many very good software engineers who dismiss it as something too complex to learn or a niche optimization meant for only the highest-performance software, not useful in everyday programming.”

#Algo DeepDive Performance

item.title: How Big Is A Git Commit?
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
How Big Is A Git Commit?

Dave Gauer

“It depends. Git stores "objects" as zlib compressed data. So the exact size of a commit will depend on the compressibility of your files (which is basically a function of the amount of repetition in them).”

#DeepDive Git
item.description: How Big Is A Git Commit?

style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Spotify does not maintain a status page, so it’s impossible to tell how widespread the outage was. I didn’t include a Spotify link in that week’s announcement either.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Outage #3 (24 June): podcast publishing broke – again. </span></strong><span>Outage #3 in five weeks; </span><em><span>deja vu</span></em><span>.  This time, it was episode publishing not working, yet again. After waiting two hours for the episode to publish on Spotify, I yet again sent out the announcement with no Spotify link.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I also emailed the Spotify Podcasts team, who confirmed the outage. I said I was considering stopping publishing video episodes, and to switch to audio-only publishing (which means pointing Spotify to my master RSS feed.) I said that an apology was appreciated but it wasn’t enough to make it worth publishing video episodes there.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>I also asked for the incident review because I had the feeling that reliability was not all that important on this podcast product. </span></strong><span>For the first outage I got a vague description of what happened, and promises of improvements that were never done – e.g. during this second outage, there was no improved communications to creators, which I was told would happen, after outage #1.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Internally, Spotify’s team surely conducted an incident review as per usual, so I figured I’d hear back in about two weeks’ time, and assumed a reply would be forthcoming because I’d made clear I was ready to leave Spotify Podcasts if reliability didn’t improve.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>No incident review three weeks later, so I quit Spotify</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The incident review had never arrived as promised by three weeks later, even though there had been time for it to be completed. auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table><figcaption class="image-caption" style="box-sizing: content-box;color: rgb(119,119,119);font-size: 14px;line-height: timeline</span></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I didn’t like how high-level </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1faf26cc-7d65-480c-8f50-7fb21bc3c095?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>the report is</span></a><span>, and how vague the promised improvements were. Specifically, this one:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“During this incident, many creators learned something was wrong from their audiences before they heard anything from us. We are improving our processes and technical capabilities so creators get notified as soon as possible when things aren’t working.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Overall, I don’t regret the choice to leave, particularly when the focus of Spotify’s leadership is on AI, not reliability.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Does Spotify have “AI psychosis?”</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Previously, I used the term “AI psychosis” differently from the usual way of describing when someone starts believing everything an AI model tells them, however outlandish. I </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/559798fe-bd24-4eef-addf-735129ce5bfb?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>applied it</span></a><span> to Meta’s rush to develop its own AI model at the cost of the reliability of its profitable business activities. This was based on Instagram’s most embarrassing-ever account takeover incident, which </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/559798fe-bd24-4eef-addf-735129ce5bfb?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>occurred</span></a><span> when the team responsible for Instagram’s Trust & Safety was slashed. Soon after, AI-generated, AI-reviewed code caused the hacking of a former US president’s account.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At Spotify, it should have gone the other way. In March, I had the opportunity to meet its Head of Technology & Platforms, Tyson Singer, who said the company puts reliability far ahead of AI adoption, and doesn’t adopt AI for its own sake. So, it was somewhat surprising to read the summary below of a podcast Spotify did </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/00857acc-6eae-44ba-9b25-ca5c33cbb443?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>with Anthropic</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Spotify now ships 4,500 production deploys a day, and 73% of PRs are now AI-assisted.</span><span><br><br><span>Niklas Gustavsson (VP of Engineering at Spotify) keeps 5 to 10 Claude sessions running in tmux, one per git worktree, agents working in the background. All of it inside a 20M+ line monorepo. He expected agents to struggle at that size, but it’s worked well.</span></span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Spotify’s migration codemods grew into thousands of lines of edge cases. Code has too much API surface for static rewrites. Early LLMs barely did better. Adding a judge took PR success from ~25% to 80%.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>All of this leans on verification, the single most important thing when agents are used and the place most companies underinvest</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Spotify rebuilt their test automation around it so engineers can confidently guide and supervise agents, rather than manually execute repetitive tasks.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It seems to me that all the talk is about </span><em><span>usage</span></em><span> of AI, and none about </span><em><span>reliability</span></em><span>, all while Spotify’s platform becomes less reliable than ever, at the same time as the streamer is going all-in on AI; with AI judges and devs running 5-10 parallel Claude sessions. A senior engineer with 5+ years of tenure at Spotify told me what’s they observe really happening at the company:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Mindless AI hype is hitting this company hard, just like it’s hitting the industry as a whole. Spotify execs have pushed people to use AI for everything even when it doesn’t make sense, so now people (particularly junior devs) started spamming AI PRs so hard that proper human reviews became unfeasible, meaning now everything gets blindly merged and as a result nothing works anymore.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I work directly with providing these pieces of AI infra so I’ve been very close to all this.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The industry as a whole is getting so ridiculous about AI,  I’m starting to think that the people who are truly passionate about engineering will eventually just cash out and either retire or build their own companies.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>All things considered, it’s worth asking if Spotify has the corporate variant of “AI psychosis”, whereby the reliability of a successful operation gets torched in the chase for the next big thing by executives. I don’t even think Spotify is all that different from Meta and other companies in this!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Things look bad, based on the quality and reliability degradation of products. Annoyingly, in many cases, customers don’t really have the choice of going elsewhere. My podcast is an exception, as video podcasts on Spotify never truly took off, so quitting the platform wasn’t a big deal. Even so, I’m particularly disappointed that Spotify has prioritized AI usage over reliability. I know some executives there pushed against this, but I feel safe in assuming that they lost that battle.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Value of staying reliable & “sucking less”</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Max Kanat-Alexander, distinguished engineer at Capital One, has </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4b4b7261-aaa2-43cc-a2aa-6e6575b29293?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>written about</span></a><span> how a software project can become wildly successful just by “sucking less” in his reflections upon the success of the Bugzilla project, (2004-2009):</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“All you have to do to succeed in software is to consistently suck less with every release.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Nobody would say that Bugzilla 2.18 was awesome, but everybody would say that it sucked less than Bugzilla 2.16 did. Bugzilla 2.20 wasn’t perfect, but without a doubt, it sucked less than Bugzilla 2.18. And then Bugzilla 3.0 fixed a whole lot of sucking in Bugzilla, and it got a whole lot more downloads.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Why is it that this worked?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As long as you consistently suck less with every release, you will retain most of your users. You’re fixing the things that bother them, so there’s no reason for them to switch away. Even if you didn’t fix everything in this release, if you sucked less, your users will have faith that eventually, the things that bother them will be fixed. New users will find your software, and they’ll stick with it too. And in this way, your user count will increase steadily over time.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>But what happens if you release frequently, but instead of fixing the things in your software that suck, you just add new features that don’t fix the sucking?</span></strong><span> Well, eventually the patience of the individual user is going to run out. They’re not going to wait forever for your software to stop sucking.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Personally, I got tired of Spotify’s Podcasts product continually going in the wrong direction on Max’s scale: the poor reliability, frequent errors on the Creators site, and the sense that they don’t really care about improving </span><em><span>existing</span></em><span> things.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>2. Will “Kimi K3 moment” trigger US push for closed-source AI models?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Chinese AI startup, Moonshot, released the latest version of their open-weight Kimi model, Kimi K3. It’s a </span><em><span>very</span></em><span> capable model that rivals Fable 5’s capabilities. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7fa2384d-ed6a-4d8b-b804-d003461640f0?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Here’s a summary</span></a><span> after benchmarking by the team at full-stack AI platform, Together AI:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“We analyzed Kimi K3 vs. Claude Fable 5 for software engineering tasks using DeepSWE.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Kimi K3 gets you the same performance as Fable 5 at ~35% of the price.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Software engineer Stephen Bochinski (ex-Google, currently Meta) is also very impressed. Last week (on 18 July), he </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a415c4cf-8780-49ad-add9-bc9c8f14e78a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>wrote</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I’ve been running Kimi K3 alongside Claude on my normal coding work, and for all practical purposes I can’t tell them apart. Same tasks, same quality of output, and near identical token counts to get there. I expected an open model to be sloppier or to grind through more tokens on the way to the same answer, and neither turned out to be true.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The prices are nowhere near each other. K3’s API runs $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output. Claude’s top model costs $10 and $50 for the same units. The subscription side is even more lopsided. Kimi’s paid plans start at $19 a month, and the $39 coding tier is far more generous than anything Claude sells anywhere near that price. Claude’s plans are metered tightly enough that a normal day of agent work can chew through the allowance before lunch.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Stephen goes into detail on how the US AI policy has been a failure: the US government blocked access to Fable, and what has been allowed to be released is an inferior version. Meanwhile, China released an equally capable, open model, available to all. Stephen </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a415c4cf-8780-49ad-add9-bc9c8f14e78a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>predicts</span></a><span> more US regulation to come:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I think I can see where this goes. The government will try to regulate AI and open source in particular, and it will run the playbook it ran for the auto industry.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Lo and behold, four days after this prediction, a science advisor to the White House accused Moonshot AI with “covert industrial distillation:”</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table When we took them apart, it was shocking what we found,” Farley told host Monica Langley in the interview.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I take the science advisor’s post above as saying that the United States strongly supports open-weight models, as long as they don’t compete with SOTA models from Anthropic or OpenAI. But now they do, so will the US restrict open-weight model usage via regulation?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Restricting the use of open models could be tricky, given Microsoft is already trialing Kimi K3 as a potential, cheaper replacement to power its Copilot AI, as reported </span><a underline;"><span>by The Information</span></a><span>,</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And it’s not just Kimi K3 as the open model href="https://substack.com/redirect/f90cd1bc-653b-4790-aca6-d095e9259344?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>on Hacker News</span></a><span> (emphasis mine):</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I’ve dealt with this error at AWS. It’s a unit error. In my case we _meant_ to charge like 5¢/GB, but </span><strong><span>missed the unit (GB), and then the billing system defaults to bytes</span></strong><span>. 5¢ per Byte of data transferred meant some customers were seeing MM bills within hours. Got paged by support around 2am, had it fixed and amendments issued by 3-4am, apology emails shortly after.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Services emit metering values that aren’t directly tied to prices. Every SKU/line item is defined in a “pricing plan”, with a unit type, regions, and price per unit. The metering records are joined to a pricing plan based on account id, region, sku, etc. Mess up the unit type in the pricing plan and the metering data conversion doesn’t work, and you get crazy bills.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It would have been nice if AWS had shared the reason for what happened, in order to allay people’s concerns, instead of turning the incorrect numbers into a joke and engagement-farming opportunity on social media.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>4. Industry Pulse</span></h2><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>OpenAI’s next model went rogue and hacked HuggingFace</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Last week, HuggingFace – the “GitHub for AI and ML models” – detected an attack on its infrastructure, which it discovered was done by an AI; specifically, OpenAI’s upcoming AI model, after it escaped its training ground. HuggingFace evaluates newly released models with its own tests and this AI wanted to hack HuggingFace to obtain test solutions in order to score better on evaluations.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s weird to even write about an AI “escaping” and hacking another service to improve its evaluation performance. But OpenAI </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0bdb2da4-8c5b-4295-9405-5db4e34303d3?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>confirmed the details</span></a><span>. Amusingly, it was a Chinese open model, GLM-5.2 that allowed HuggingFace to defend itself, after models like OpenAI refused to help mitigate the attack. From the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3d7324e6-d4fc-4015-b415-f1704378e8e7?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>incident report by HuggingFace</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“When we started the log analysis, we first used frontier models behind commercial APIs. This did not work: the analysis requires submitting large volumes of real attack commands, exploit payloads, and C2 artifacts, and these requests were blocked by the providers’ safety guardrails, which cannot distinguish an incident responder from an attacker. We ran the forensic analysis instead on GLM 5.2, an open-weight model, on our own infrastructure. This had a second benefit: no attacker data, and none of the credentials it referenced, left our environment.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This attack makes the case quite strongly for why open models are so useful in cybersecurity. And it’s ironic that OpenAI likely blocked HuggingFace’s analysis of the attack by OpenAI’s own model! The full report from HuggingFace is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3d7324e6-d4fc-4015-b415-f1704378e8e7?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>well worth a read.</span></a></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>X takes more than a year to build Android app</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Perhaps building software is not so much faster when engineers use AI for coding, after all, judging by the social networking site, X, whose team </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0e488a61-ff29-4ed6-9c83-cc3b418c1cc3?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>took more than a year</span></a><span> to rebuild its Android app from scratch. After that, the new app still lacks features the iOS app has, like hosting Spaces.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I appreciate the transparency on how long building this app took. On the one hand, AI coding tools are not as effective with native Android and iOS as they are on the web. But even so, it’s a reminder that building (or rebuilding) complex software products takes time, especially when aiming for a quality result.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position:
